DiffGIPC: Differentiable Mixed-Coordinate Contact Dynamics on GPU

Journal: TOGCCS: Computing methodologies Physical simulationCCS: Computing methodologies Parallel algorithms
Kemeng Huang email: kmhuang@connect.hku.hk email: kmhuang819@gmail.com Affiliation: The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China , Bowen Ren email: boweyna@gmail.com Affiliation: The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China , Xinyu Lu email: lxy819469559@gmail.com Affiliation: TransGP, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China , Minchen Li email: minchernl@gmail.com Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, USA and Taku Komura email: taku@cs.hku.hk Affiliation: The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
© none
Abstract.

Contact-rich inverse problems require efficient gradients and reliable enforcement of non-penetration. Existing differentiable methods provide fast simulation and rigid-deformable coupling, but contact treatments based on penalties or velocity-level constraints can permit penetration or positional drift. Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) maintains non-penetration through geometric barriers and continuous collision detection (CCD). However, repeated forward and backward evaluations remain costly in full-space finite-element (FEM) implementations, particularly when nearly rigid components retain many vertex degrees of freedom (DoFs). We present DiffGIPC, a GPU-accelerated differentiable IPC framework for optimizing interacting deformable and nearly rigid bodies. Our affine-body derivatives enable rest-shape design, initial-state optimization, and articulated control while retaining only twelve motion DoFs per affine body. These gradients account for how changes in geometry, placement, and actuation affect other objects through collision and friction. We preserve these interactions in one coupled FEM-affine adjoint system per frame, reducing the backward-system size without discarding the dependencies that drive the inverse problem. GPU-optimized backward computation further reduces the cost of repeated gradient evaluations. A reusable PyTorch interface connects supported physical parameters to user-defined parameter maps and losses across design, identification, motion, placement, and articulated control. Experiments demonstrate peak speedups over DiffIPC of approximately 150.0×150.0\times with full-space FEM and 4133.3×4133.3\times with affine bodies for combined forward simulation and backward differentiation.

Keywords: 
differentiable simulation, contact, affine body dynamics, finite elements, GPU simulation, articulated control, inverse design

1. Introduction

Gradient-based design, system identification, and control often optimize one object’s parameters for their effect on another object. A hanger’s shape determines whether a garment remains supported. An initial velocity determines where another body moves after collision, and a robot command changes the motion of a grasped deformable object. In each case, the gradient must follow forces transmitted through contact and the subsequent motion. Computing these derivatives efficiently is particularly challenging when a scene combines deformable objects with detailed, nearly rigid components: the representation must resolve the interactions without making every stiff component expensive to differentiate.

Existing methods address different parts of this problem. Differentiable projective-dynamics methods, including DiffPD and DiffCloth (Du et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022), accelerate repeated solves through local-global iterations and matrix prefactorization. Representing nearly rigid components as stiff deformable meshes nevertheless retains vertex-level motion DoFs, increasing simulation and differentiation costs even when only near-rigid motion is required (Lai et al., 2026). ADD (Geilinger et al., 2020) provides fully implicit, two-way coupled rigid and deformable dynamics with analytic adjoints, but uses penalty-based normal contact, which does not strictly prevent interpenetration. DiffIPC (Huang et al., 2024c) differentiates fully implicit FEM dynamics with friction, using IPC barriers and continuous collision detection to maintain non-penetration. Its full-space representation, however, carries the motion DoFs of every stiff component into the backward solve, making repeated evaluations costly in its CPU implementation. The resulting opportunity is to combine contact-coupled differentiation with compact motion coordinates and efficient GPU execution.

We present DiffGIPC, a GPU-accelerated framework for differentiating coupled FEM-affine IPC simulations (Figure 2). Building on the forward formulation of StiffGIPC (Huang et al., 2025a), we derive frame-wise adjoints directly in the mixed motion coordinates. Full-space FEM retains the freedom needed for local deformation, while each affine body contributes only twelve motion DoFs regardless of its surface resolution. Contact and joint derivatives couple interacting bodies within each frame. Inertia and friction make the time integration equations depend on earlier states. The backward systems therefore remain compact while preserving cross-object coupling and the temporal dependencies required for coupled inverse problems.

Compact motion coordinates alone do not provide shape or control gradients. Changing an affine rest surface changes its mass, the positions at which contact is evaluated, and the maps that convert point-space forces to affine coordinates. Under friction, the same rest change also moves the previous-frame points used to define sliding and the lagged contact quantities. We differentiate these dependencies explicitly, together with initial states and revolute or prismatic joint controls, and accumulate them in parallel without enlarging the adjoint system. To retain the advantage of compact systems, conditional CUDA Graphs are employed to keep preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) iterations and convergence checks on the GPU, thereby reducing the overhead of repeated kernel launches and CPU–GPU synchronization. A PyTorch interface connects these physical gradients to user-defined parameter maps and losses.

In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    Coupled FEM-affine adjoints for differentiable IPC. We derive trajectory adjoints in mixed FEM and affine coordinates, preserving contact, friction, and joint coupling while using only twelve motion DoFs per affine body.

  • •

    Affine-body derivatives for shape design and articulated control. We derive gradients for affine rest shapes, initial states, and joint controls, including shape-dependent inertia and frictional contact.

  • •

    A reusable GPU optimization pipeline. We develop a GPU-parallel adjoint and gradient-accumulation pipeline with conditional CUDA Graphs and a PyTorch interface for design, system identification, and control.

  • •

    Fully GPU-parallel differentiable IPC. We present the first fully GPU-parallel differentiable IPC framework for coupled nearly rigid and deformable bodies, with substantial speedups demonstrated across contact-rich inverse problems.

Our evaluation examines the benefits of GPU execution and compact motion representations across contact-rich inverse problems. For comparison with DiffIPC, we retain full-space FEM in both systems and use relatively low-resolution benchmarks to keep evaluation times manageable for the CPU-based baseline. Even at these resolutions, DiffGIPC achieves 12.312.3–34.1×34.1\times speedups in complete backward evaluation and 10.610.6–60.9×60.9\times speedups in combined forward and backward evaluation, covering initial motion, rest shape, material, and friction optimization. A separate resolution study examines how performance scales with geometric detail and the additional benefit of affine coordinates. Further experiments demonstrate cloth design, affine shape optimization, stable placement, and articulated control. The source code of our framework will be released.

2. Related Work

Efficient differentiable simulation and contact

Inverse problems such as parameter identification from measured motion (Hahn et al., 2019; Jatavallabhula et al., 2021) require repeated simulation and gradient evaluations, making the efficiency of both computations important. DiffTaichi automates the differentiation of parallel simulation programs through source-code transformations (Hu et al., 2020). Brax integrates differentiable rigid-body simulation and learning on accelerators, reducing data transfer between simulation and optimization (Freeman et al., 2021). ChainQueen (Hu et al., 2019) uses explicit MLS-MPM with parallel local updates, but stiff materials require small time steps. Implicit deformable simulation methods (Rojas et al., 2021; Liang et al., 2019; Li et al., 2026) offer greater time-step stability, at the cost of solving linear systems during both simulation and differentiation. Projective dynamics (PD) reduces this cost through local projections and a global system whose matrix can be prefactorized for fixed discretization and coefficients (Bouaziz et al., 2014). DiffPD reuses this factorization in its backward iterations (Du et al., 2021). Quasi-Newton methods support more general hyperelastic energies through efficient approximate systems (Liu et al., 2017), and DiffQN further reduces differentiation costs by reusing factorizations from the forward simulation (Cai et al., 2025). More recently, DiffPhD combines GPU factor reuse with techniques for heterogeneous and hyperelastic materials (Lai et al., 2026).

For contact-rich inverse problems, these computational benefits must also be considered alongside the contact response being differentiated. DiffPD’s penalty formulation supports frictional sliding but permits interpenetration, whereas its complementarity formulation enforces non-penetration under a sticky-contact assumption (Du et al., 2021). DiffCloth differentiates the dry-friction PD formulation of Ly et al. (2020), supporting sliding cloth contact (Li et al., 2022). However, its self-collision treatment considers only vertex-vertex pairs and does not handle vertex-face or edge-edge self-collisions. DiffPhD supports Signorini-Coulomb contact on the GPU, but its velocity-level enforcement can produce position drift under quasi-static support (Lai et al., 2026). These limitations are particularly relevant when the optimized behavior depends on sustained support, sliding, or contact between thin surfaces. They motivate efficient differentiation of contact models that preserve geometric non-penetration throughout the simulated motion.

Differentiable contact and coupled dynamics

Qiao et al. (2020) enable differentiable two-way coupling between rigid bodies and cloth, using local impact zones to reduce the cost of collision handling and differentiation. ADD provides fully implicit rigid-deformable coupling with analytic adjoints (Geilinger et al., 2020). Its normal penalty makes contact differentiable while allowing finite overlap. Increasing the penalty stiffness reduces overlap at the cost of poorer conditioning. IPC instead combines a geometric barrier with continuous collision detection to maintain intersection-free motion from feasible initial configurations (Li et al., 2020). DiffIPC brings this contact model to differentiable FEM simulation and supports shape, material, friction, and initial-state optimization (Huang et al., 2024c). It therefore provides a strong basis for inverse problems in which penetration would change the intended interaction. However, representing nearly rigid components with highly stiff, full-space FEM retains vertex-level motion DoFs even when their local deformation is negligible. In its CPU-based implementation, repeated simulation and differentiation of these large systems remain costly. DiffGIPC addresses this cost with coupled FEM-ABD adjoints and GPU backward computation while retaining IPC’s geometric contact safeguards.

Compact coordinates for coupled design and control

Reducing motion DoFs addresses a cost that faster linear algebra alone does not remove. Modal and adaptive subspaces reduce deformable motion to a smaller set of directions (Barbič and James, 2005; Trusty et al., 2024). Their accuracy depends on whether those directions capture the deformation induced by loads and contact. Hyper-reduced PD also approximates local constraint projections (Brandt et al., 2018), while subspace mixed FEM combines reduced positions with stretch variables to handle heterogeneous materials (Trusty et al., 2023). These approaches retain selected deformation modes and reduce their evaluation cost. For components whose internal deformation is negligible, rigid-body coordinates avoid resolving these modes altogether. Rigid IPC preserves non-penetration in this representation by accounting for curved rotational trajectories in collision detection (Ferguson et al., 2021). ABD relaxes exact rigidity through a stiff orthogonality energy and uses twelve affine DoFs per body (Lan et al., 2022). Its surface positions are linear in these DoFs, allowing piecewise-linear collision trajectories and a pose-independent mass matrix at fixed rest geometry. This offers a compact representation for stiff parts, while full-space FEM retains local deformation where it is needed. DiffGIPC carries both representations into the same backward system, retaining contact, friction, and joint coupling between bodies.

Compact rigid-body states have supported differentiable learning and control (Belbute-Peres et al., 2018; Degrave et al., 2019), including articulated dynamics in Nimble (Werling et al., 2021). Shape optimization requires an additional distinction between the motion representation and the geometry being designed. Contact-based assemblies and shock-protecting microstructures (Tozoni et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2024b) use geometric changes to alter load transfer and contact-dependent mechanical response. Pneumatic actuator design and garment reconstruction (Gjoka et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025) likewise optimize rest geometry through its effect on deformation. These applications motivate retaining a rich design space even when the motion state can be compact.

SDRS uses convex polyhedra and auxiliary separating planes to maintain differentiability under large shape changes (Ye et al., 2025). Our focus is mesh-based design and control of affine bodies interacting with deformable objects under IPC. Affine rest-shape changes affect both the mass matrix and the maps from affine DoFs to surface points. Differentiating these dependencies allows a body’s shape to be optimized for its frictional interactions with other objects. Derivatives of joint targets and forces likewise account for the coupled response of articulated and deformable bodies. For a fixed motion representation, additional design parameters do not enlarge the per-frame backward system. Each affine body therefore contributes only twelve motion DoFs, even when its rest shape is described by many design parameters. Contact processing still depends on surface resolution, while parameter-gradient evaluation requires additional work as the number of design parameters grows.

GPU computation for trajectory adjoints

Compact coordinates reduce adjoint system size, while efficient linear solvers further reduce the cost of trajectory differentiation. PD-based local-global methods exploit a fixed global matrix to reuse precomputed factors. Zeng et al. (2025) use a sparse representation of its inverse to accelerate GPU forward simulation. DiffPhD adopts this strategy for differentiable simulation, reusing an inverse factor across forward, backward, and frictional-contact computations (Lai et al., 2026). In IPC, however, the frame Hessian varies with deformation and contact, so a fixed factorization cannot be reused across all adjoint systems along a trajectory. Preconditioned iterative solvers provide an alternative, with effective preconditioning reducing the number of iterations (Chen et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2022). GIPC parallelizes IPC computation (Huang et al., 2024a), while StiffGIPC provides efficient FEM-ABD coupling and GPU solvers across a wide range of stiffnesses (Huang et al., 2025a), and AGIPC further reduces GPU linear-solve costs through adaptive in-solve algebraic coarsening (Wang et al., 2026). These methods advance GPU IPC efficiency, with StiffGIPC supplying the forward simulation foundation for our work.

DiffGIPC combines coupled frame-wise adjoint solves with parallel gradient accumulation on the GPU. Compact affine coordinates reduce PCG’s numerical workload, making repeated CPU kernel launches and convergence synchronization more prominent. Conditional CUDA Graphs reduce this overhead by keeping iteration control and convergence checks on the GPU, with compatible graphs reused across frames as the Hessian changes. After each solve, local derivative products are accumulated in parallel to compute physical-parameter gradients and update earlier-frame adjoint right-hand sides.

3. A Unified Differentiable IPC Framework

The framework separates the coordinates needed to describe contact geometry from those needed to solve motion. Collision and friction derivatives are evaluated at world-space surface points and mapped into a coupled system of FEM vertex positions and affine body coordinates. This preserves cross-object derivatives while assigning twelve motion DoFs to each affine body.

The forward formulation builds on StiffGIPC (Huang et al., 2025a). Simulation DoFs describe solved motion, whereas physical parameters are inputs changed by the optimizer. One frame is an accepted time step of length hh, and mesh connectivity is fixed within each differentiated trajectory. The state and incremental potential below define the single-step adjoint. Section 4 extends it through time, Section 5 supplies affine design and control derivatives, and Section 6 develops their GPU computation and task interface.

3.3. Parameter gradients from the step equation

Consider first a single time step from a prescribed initial state, omitting the frame index. The solved DoFs satisfy 𝐠⁡(𝐲,𝜽)=𝟎\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{y},\boldsymbol{\theta})=\mathbf{0}. (9) ∂𝐠∂𝐲⏟𝐇​d​𝐲d​𝜽+∂𝐠∂𝜽⏟𝐆=𝟎.\underbrace{\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}}{\partial\mathbf{y}}}_{\mathbf{H}}\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}}{\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}}+\underbrace{\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}}}_{\mathbf{G}}=\mathbf{0}.

Here, 𝐆\mathbf{G} is the partial derivative of the energy gradient with respect to the physical parameters. The derivative 𝐇\mathbf{H} with respect to the DoFs is the Hessian of the incremental potential:

(10) 𝐇=∂𝐠∂𝐲=∇𝐲2Φ.\mathbf{H}=\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}}{\partial\mathbf{y}}=\nabla_{\mathbf{y}}^{2}\Phi.

Both matrices are evaluated at the converged DoFs satisfying 𝐠⁡(𝐲,𝜽)=𝟎\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{y},\boldsymbol{\theta})=\mathbf{0}. Rather than forming d​𝐲/d​𝜽\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}/\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta} explicitly, we use the adjoint below. Restoring the frame index, we denote these matrices by 𝐇t∈ℝn×n\mathbf{H}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} and 𝐆t∈ℝn×nθ\mathbf{G}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n_{\theta}}.

For a scalar loss L⁡(𝐲,𝜽)L(\mathbf{y},\boldsymbol{\theta}), let ℓy=∇𝐲L\boldsymbol{\ell}_{y}=\nabla_{\mathbf{y}}L and ℓθ=∇𝜽L\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta}=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}L denote its partial gradients with respect to the DoFs and physical parameters, respectively. The chain rule gives

(11) ∇𝜽L=ℓθ+(d​𝐲d​𝜽)𝖳​ℓy.\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}L=\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta}+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}}{\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\ell}_{y}.

Explicitly computing d​𝐲/d​𝜽\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}/\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta} becomes costly as the number of optimized parameters grows. We avoid forming this matrix and compute the loss gradient by solving the adjoint system:

(12) 𝐇𝖳​𝝀=ℓy.\mathbf{H}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}=\boldsymbol{\ell}_{y}.

The solution 𝝀\boldsymbol{\lambda} is the adjoint vector. Combining this solve with Equation (9) gives the parameter gradient

(13) ∇𝜽L=ℓθ−𝐆𝖳​𝝀.\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}L=\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta}-\mathbf{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}.

For a single time step, all parameter gradients share the same coupled FEM-affine adjoint. Section 4 extends this formulation through time.

3.4. Collision and friction derivatives across representations

Collision and friction energies are evaluated at world-space surface points, whereas the adjoint in Equation (12) acts on simulation DoFs. The map 𝐊t,c\mathbf{K}_{t,c} from Equation (5) converts the point-space derivatives into FEM and affine coordinates. The collision energy uses GIPC’s squared-log barrier on squared distance (Huang et al., 2024a)

(14) bbar​(d)={κ​(d−d^)2​log2⁡(d/d^),0<d<d^,0,d≥d^,b_{\mathrm{bar}}(d)=\begin{cases}\kappa(d-\widehat{d})^{2}\log^{2}(d/\widehat{d}),&0<d<\widehat{d},\\ 0,&d\geq\widehat{d},\end{cases}

where dd is the squared distance, d^\widehat{d} is its activation threshold, and κ\kappa is the barrier coefficient. This squared-log form is the GIPC barrier, rather than the original IPC single-log form. At each Newton iteration, we truncate the step along the search direction using continuous collision detection to prevent intersections, followed by line search to ensure a decrease in the incremental potential. Backward differentiation uses the converged frame state and its associated collision and friction data.

For a contact cc at frame tt, let 𝐠t,cx\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{x} and 𝐇t,cx\mathbf{H}_{t,c}^{x} denote the gradient and Hessian of the collision energy with respect to the stacked world-space point positions 𝐱tc\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}. The superscript xx denotes point coordinates, whereas yy denotes simulation DoFs. With rest geometry fixed, the point map 𝐊t,c\mathbf{K}_{t,c} from Equation (5) is constant with respect to 𝐲t\mathbf{y}_{t}. The chain rule therefore gives the contributions to the frame energy gradient and Hessian:

(15) 𝐠t,cy=𝐊t,c𝖳​𝐠t,cx,𝐇t,cy=𝐊t,c𝖳​𝐇t,cx​𝐊t,c.\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{y}=\mathbf{K}_{t,c}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{x},\qquad\mathbf{H}_{t,c}^{y}=\mathbf{K}_{t,c}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{H}_{t,c}^{x}\mathbf{K}_{t,c}.

The same transformation applies to friction derivatives with respect to the current-frame DoFs. Friction derivatives with respect to earlier states are included in the trajectory calculation in Section 4.

Each point contributes through the map associated with its object. For point ii on affine body bb and point jj on affine body b′b^{\prime}, let 𝐇i​jx\mathbf{H}_{ij}^{x} be their 3×33\times 3 point-space Hessian block. Mapping this block gives a 12×1212\times 12 contribution to 𝐇b​b′AA\mathbf{H}_{bb^{\prime}}^{\mathrm{AA}}. If the second point is instead a FEM vertex jj, its identity map gives a 12×312\times 3 contribution to 𝐇b​jAF\mathbf{H}_{bj}^{\mathrm{AF}}. For the point pair (i,j)(i,j), the block contributions are

(16) Δ​𝐇b​b′AA,(i,j)\displaystyle\Delta\mathbf{H}_{bb^{\prime}}^{\mathrm{AA},(i,j)} =𝐉i𝖳​𝐇i​jx​𝐉j,\displaystyle=\mathbf{J}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{H}_{ij}^{x}\mathbf{J}_{j},
Δ​𝐇b​jAF,(i,j)\displaystyle\Delta\mathbf{H}_{bj}^{\mathrm{AF},(i,j)} =𝐉i𝖳​𝐇i​jx.\displaystyle=\mathbf{J}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{H}_{ij}^{x}.

All surface vertices of an affine body share its twelve DoFs. The contributions of all relevant point pairs are summed into the corresponding body blocks, without introducing independent vertex DoFs. For distinct points on the same body, both ordered point-block contributions must be included when they map to the same diagonal body block.

After assembly, grouping affine (A\mathrm{A}) and finite-element (F\mathrm{F}) DoFs gives the frame Hessian

(17) 𝐇t=[𝐇AA𝐇AF𝐇FA𝐇FF],𝐇FA=𝐇AF𝖳.\mathbf{H}_{t}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{AA}}&\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{AF}}\\ \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{FA}}&\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{FF}}\end{bmatrix},\qquad\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{FA}}=\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{AF}}^{\mathsf{T}}.

The diagonal blocks 𝐇AA\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{AA}} and 𝐇FF\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{FF}} collect derivatives within the affine and FEM coordinates. Collision and friction contribute 𝐇AF\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{AF}} and 𝐇FA\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{FA}}, while joints couple affine bodies within 𝐇AA\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{AA}}. These cross blocks let a loss on one object influence parameters of another. Compact affine coordinates reduce system size while the cross terms preserve the interacting response.

The same point maps form the loss-gradient vector ℓy\boldsymbol{\ell}_{y} on the right-hand side of Equation (12). For a loss evaluated on world-space surface points, its gradient with respect to the affine coordinates of body bb, whose surface-vertex index set is 𝒱b\mathcal{V}_{b}, is

(18) ∇𝐪bL=∑i∈𝒱b𝐉i𝖳​∇𝐱iL.\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{b}}L=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{V}_{b}}\mathbf{J}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{i}}L.

For a FEM vertex, the loss gradient with respect to its DoFs equals that with respect to its world-space position. These mappings hold with rest geometry fixed. Section 5.2 includes the additional dependence of the point maps and surface positions on rest shape. Section 4 extends this coupled adjoint to trajectories, where earlier states affect both later motion and the loss.

4. Frame-Wise Adjoint

The single-step adjoint captures interactions at one frame. A trajectory also depends on how earlier motion changes later inertia and friction. We account for these dependencies by backward substitution through the causal sequence of frame equations. Each reverse frame solves one coupled FEM-affine system, then contributes to the parameters and earlier states that influenced it. Algorithm 1 summarizes this recurrence. We derive its temporal structure and then specify the inertia and friction terms, using the converged states and recorded data that define the forward equations.

4.1. Equations for the whole trajectory

Let 𝐲t∈ℝn\mathbf{y}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} contain the free simulation DoFs in the order defined in Section 3.1. The equation at frame tt depends on its current state, a subset of earlier solved states, and the physical parameters:

(19) 𝐠t​(𝐲t,{𝐲s:s∈𝒟⁡(t)},𝜽)=𝟎.\mathbf{g}_{t}(\mathbf{y}_{t},\{\mathbf{y}_{s}:s\in\mathcal{D}(t)\},\boldsymbol{\theta})=\mathbf{0}.

The set 𝒟⁡(t)⊆{1,…,t−1}\mathcal{D}(t)\subseteq\{1,\ldots,t-1\} identifies those earlier frames. The initial state is an input rather than a solved frame: its optimized components contribute to 𝐆t\mathbf{G}_{t}, while unselected components remain fixed. Prescribed joint commands likewise enter 𝐆t\mathbf{G}_{t} through the applied controls. The matrices 𝐇t\mathbf{H}_{t} and 𝐆t\mathbf{G}_{t} retain their state and parameter definitions from Section 3.3. Temporal dependence introduces the additional derivative

(20) 𝐂t,s=∂𝐠t∂𝐲s∈ℝn×n,s∈𝒟⁡(t).\mathbf{C}_{t,s}=\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}_{t}}{\partial\mathbf{y}_{s}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n},\qquad s\in\mathcal{D}(t).

Thus 𝐇t\mathbf{H}_{t} describes the coupled response within frame tt, whereas 𝐂t,s\mathbf{C}_{t,s} describes its dependence on an earlier state and vanishes for s∉𝒟⁡(t)s\notin\mathcal{D}(t). Both current and earlier solved states vary with 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}. Differentiating Equation (19) includes these changes together with the direct parameter derivative:

(21) 𝐇t​d​𝐲td​𝜽+∑s∈𝒟⁡(t)𝐂t,s​d​𝐲sd​𝜽+𝐆t=0.\mathbf{H}_{t}\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}}+\sum_{s\in\mathcal{D}(t)}\mathbf{C}_{t,s}\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}_{s}}{\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}}+\mathbf{G}_{t}=0.

With 𝐒t=d​𝐲t/d​𝜽∈ℝn×nθ\mathbf{S}_{t}=\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}_{t}/\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n_{\theta}}, the equations for all frames form the block system

(22) [𝐇10⋯0𝐂2,1𝐇2⋱⋱⋱0𝐂T,1⋯𝐂T,T−1𝐇T]⏟𝓙​[𝐒1𝐒2𝐒T]⏟𝓢=−[𝐆1𝐆2𝐆T]⏟𝓖.\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{H}_{1}&0&\cdots&0\\ \mathbf{C}_{2,1}&\mathbf{H}_{2}&\ddots&\vdots\\ \vdots&\ddots&\ddots&0\\ \mathbf{C}_{T,1}&\cdots&\mathbf{C}_{T,T-1}&\mathbf{H}_{T}\end{bmatrix}}_{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{J}}}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{S}_{1}\\ \mathbf{S}_{2}\\ \vdots\\ \mathbf{S}_{T}\end{bmatrix}}_{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}}=-\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{G}_{1}\\ \mathbf{G}_{2}\\ \vdots\\ \mathbf{G}_{T}\end{bmatrix}}_{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}}.

Causality makes 𝓙\boldsymbol{\mathcal{J}} block lower triangular, with the frame Hessians 𝐇t\mathbf{H}_{t} on the diagonal and nonzero off-diagonal blocks only for dependencies in 𝒟⁡(t)\mathcal{D}(t).

The predictor in Equation (7) depends on 𝐲t−1\mathbf{y}_{t-1} and 𝐲t−2\mathbf{y}_{t-2}. Friction adds to the first of these dependencies, through 𝐂t,t−1\mathbf{C}_{t,t-1}. For the first three solved frames, the system is

(23) [𝐇100𝐂2,1𝐇20𝐂3,1𝐂3,2𝐇3]​[𝐒1𝐒2𝐒3]=−[𝐆1𝐆2𝐆3].\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{H}_{1}&0&0\\ \mathbf{C}_{2,1}&\mathbf{H}_{2}&0\\ \mathbf{C}_{3,1}&\mathbf{C}_{3,2}&\mathbf{H}_{3}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{S}_{1}\\ \mathbf{S}_{2}\\ \mathbf{S}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=-\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{G}_{1}\\ \mathbf{G}_{2}\\ \mathbf{G}_{3}\end{bmatrix}.

This three-frame system illustrates the reverse calculation below. The sensitivities 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t} and the assembled trajectory matrix are used for the derivation, but are not formed by the backward algorithm.

4.2. Reverse-time adjoint equations

We extend the single-step adjoint in Equation (12) to the trajectory loss L⁡(𝐲1,…,𝐲T,𝜽)L(\mathbf{y}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{y}_{T};\boldsymbol{\theta}). Let ℓt=∇𝐲tL\boldsymbol{\ell}_{t}=\nabla_{\mathbf{y}_{t}}L denote its partial gradient with respect to the simulation DoFs at frame tt, and let ℓθ\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta} denote its partial parameter gradient with all simulated states fixed. For a loss evaluated only on the final state, ℓt=𝟎\boldsymbol{\ell}_{t}=\mathbf{0} for t<Tt<T, although earlier states can still affect the loss through the subsequent motion. Using 𝐒t=d​𝐲t/d​𝜽\mathbf{S}_{t}=\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}_{t}/\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta} from Section 4.1, the chain rule extends Equation (11) to

(24) ∇𝜽L\displaystyle\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}L =ℓθ+∑t=1T(d​𝐲td​𝜽)𝖳​ℓt\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\ell}_{t}
=ℓθ+∑t=1T𝐒t𝖳​ℓt\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\ell}_{t}
=ℓθ+𝓢𝖳​ℓall,\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta}+\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\mathrm{all}},

where ℓall\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\mathrm{all}} stacks the per-frame loss gradients in the same order as the blocks of 𝓢\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}. The first term accounts for the explicit parameter dependence of the loss. The second accounts for changes in the simulated trajectory.

To evaluate the trajectory contribution without computing 𝓢\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}, we introduce an adjoint vector 𝝀t\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t} for each frame and solve

(25) 𝓙𝖳​[𝝀1𝝀T]⏟𝚲=[ℓ1ℓT]⏟ℓall.\boldsymbol{\mathcal{J}}^{\mathsf{T}}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{1}\\ \vdots\\ \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{T}\end{bmatrix}}_{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\ell}_{1}\\ \vdots\\ \boldsymbol{\ell}_{T}\end{bmatrix}}_{\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\mathrm{all}}}.

Combining this equation with 𝓙​𝓢=−𝓖\boldsymbol{\mathcal{J}}\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}=-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}} from Equation (22) gives

(26) 𝓢𝖳​ℓall=𝓢𝖳​𝓙𝖳​𝚲=−𝓖𝖳​𝚲.\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\mathrm{all}}=\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\mathcal{J}}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}.

The transpose reverses the causal order: 𝓙𝖳\boldsymbol{\mathcal{J}}^{\mathsf{T}} is block upper triangular, so the trajectory adjoint is solved from the last frame backward. For the three-frame example,

(27) [𝐇1𝖳𝐂2,1𝖳𝐂3,1𝖳0𝐇2𝖳𝐂3,2𝖳00𝐇3𝖳]​[𝝀1𝝀2𝝀3]=[ℓ1ℓ2ℓ3].\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{H}_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}&\mathbf{C}_{2,1}^{\mathsf{T}}&\mathbf{C}_{3,1}^{\mathsf{T}}\\ 0&\mathbf{H}_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}&\mathbf{C}_{3,2}^{\mathsf{T}}\\ 0&0&\mathbf{H}_{3}^{\mathsf{T}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{1}\\ \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{2}\\ \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\ell}_{1}\\ \boldsymbol{\ell}_{2}\\ \boldsymbol{\ell}_{3}\end{bmatrix}.

Backward substitution first determines 𝝀3\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{3}, then includes its effect when solving for the earlier adjoints:

𝐇3𝖳​𝝀3\displaystyle\mathbf{H}_{3}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{3} =ℓ3,\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\ell}_{3},
𝐇2𝖳​𝝀2\displaystyle\mathbf{H}_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{2} =ℓ2−𝐂3,2𝖳​𝝀3,\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\ell}_{2}-\mathbf{C}_{3,2}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{3},
(28) 𝐇1𝖳​𝝀1\displaystyle\mathbf{H}_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{1} =ℓ1−𝐂2,1𝖳​𝝀2−𝐂3,1𝖳​𝝀3.\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\ell}_{1}-\mathbf{C}_{2,1}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{2}-\mathbf{C}_{3,1}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{3}.

Applying the same backward substitution to all TT frames gives

(29) 𝐇t𝖳𝝀t=ℓt−∑τ>tt∈𝒟⁡(τ)𝐂τ,t𝖳𝝀τ,t=T,…,1.\mathbf{H}_{t}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t}=\boldsymbol{\ell}_{t}-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\tau>t\\ t\in\mathcal{D}(\tau)\end{subarray}}\mathbf{C}_{\tau,t}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\tau},\qquad t=T,\ldots,1.

Only later equations that depend on 𝐲t\mathbf{y}_{t} contribute to its right-hand side. The resulting adjoints account for these temporal effects in the parameter gradient:

(30) ∇𝜽L\displaystyle\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}L =ℓθ−𝓖𝖳​𝚲\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
=ℓθ−∑t=1T𝐆t𝖳​𝝀t.\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta}-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf{G}_{t}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t}.

4.3. Computing one coupled system per frame

For each frame tt, 𝐛t\mathbf{b}_{t} denotes the right-hand side of its adjoint equation. The vector 𝜽¯\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}} accumulates contributions to the loss gradient with respect to the physical parameters 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}. The reverse pass starts from the direct loss derivatives, 𝐛t=ℓt\mathbf{b}_{t}=\boldsymbol{\ell}_{t} for t=1,…,Tt=1,\ldots,T and 𝜽¯=ℓθ\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}=\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta}. Before frame tt is solved, 𝐛t\mathbf{b}_{t} combines the direct loss gradient with respect to its motion DoFs 𝐲t\mathbf{y}_{t} with all contributions propagated from later frames that depend on 𝐲t\mathbf{y}_{t}. The backward pass processes frames in reverse order. For each frame, 𝐇t\mathbf{H}_{t} is first assembled from that frame’s saved converged state. The adjoint is then obtained by solving

(31) 𝐇t𝖳​𝝀t=𝐛t.\mathbf{H}_{t}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t}=\mathbf{b}_{t}.

Let Δ​𝐛s(t)\Delta\mathbf{b}_{s}^{(t)} and Δ​𝜽¯(t)\Delta\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(t)} denote frame tt’s contributions to an earlier-frame right-hand side and the parameter gradient, respectively. They are given by

(32) Δ​𝐛s(t)\displaystyle\Delta\mathbf{b}_{s}^{(t)} =−𝐂t,s𝖳​𝝀t,\displaystyle=-\mathbf{C}_{t,s}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t}, s∈𝒟⁡(t),\displaystyle s\in\mathcal{D}(t),
(33) Δ​𝜽¯(t)\displaystyle\Delta\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(t)} =−𝐆t𝖳​𝝀t.\displaystyle=-\mathbf{G}_{t}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t}.

The history contributions are summed into the corresponding 𝐛s\mathbf{b}_{s}, giving the right-hand side in Equation (29). The parameter contributions are summed into 𝜽¯\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}. After all frames have been processed, 𝜽¯=∇𝜽L\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}L, as given by Equation (30).

Each history contribution reaches frame s<ts<t before that frame is solved (Figure 3). The products in Equations (32) and (33) are evaluated locally without assembling full 𝐂t,s\mathbf{C}_{t,s} or 𝐆t\mathbf{G}_{t}. Only the current frame’s Hessian is retained during this reverse traversal, together with the saved trajectory and accumulated right-hand sides.

Each retained 𝐇t\mathbf{H}_{t} preserves cross-object coupling, while backward substitution carries that response through time. The trajectory length determines the number of frame solves. Additional parameters contribute local derivative products and share these solves, making the same recurrence suitable for low-dimensional controls and detailed shape design.

4.4. Inertia and initial-state dependencies

The history contribution in Equation (32) requires the derivative of 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t} with respect to each earlier state. For inertia, 𝐠tin=𝐌⁡(𝐲t−𝐲^t)\mathbf{g}_{t}^{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{y}_{t}-\widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{t}). Substituting the BDF1 predictor from Equation (7) and differentiating with respect to 𝐲t−1\mathbf{y}_{t-1} and 𝐲t−2\mathbf{y}_{t-2} gives

(34) 𝐂t,t−1in=−2​𝐌,𝐂t,t−2in=𝐌.\mathbf{C}_{t,t-1}^{\mathrm{in}}=-2{\mathbf{M}},\qquad\mathbf{C}_{t,t-2}^{\mathrm{in}}={\mathbf{M}}.

Substituting these blocks into Equation (32) gives the inertial parts of Δ​𝐛s(t)\Delta\mathbf{b}_{s}^{(t)}, denoted by the superscript in\mathrm{in}:

(35) Δ​𝐛t−1(t),in\displaystyle\Delta\mathbf{b}_{t-1}^{(t),\mathrm{in}} =2​𝐌​𝝀t,\displaystyle=2\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t}, t≥2,\displaystyle t\geq 2,
Δ​𝐛t−2(t),in\displaystyle\Delta\mathbf{b}_{t-2}^{(t),\mathrm{in}} =−𝐌​𝝀t,\displaystyle=-\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t}, t≥3.\displaystyle t\geq 3.

The same mass products apply to both representations: 𝐌\mathbf{M} contains the FEM vertex-mass blocks and the 12×1212\times 12 mass block of each affine body.

The initial configuration and velocity are inputs to the simulation, not additional solved frames. Their contributions therefore enter the parameter-gradient contribution in Equation (33), rather than a right-hand-side vector 𝐛0\mathbf{b}_{0}. The first-step predictor is 𝐲^1=𝐲0+h​𝐲˙0+h2​𝐚1\widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{1}=\mathbf{y}_{0}+h\dot{\mathbf{y}}_{0}+h^{2}\mathbf{a}_{1}, so the inertial derivatives with respect to 𝐲0\mathbf{y}_{0} and 𝐲˙0\dot{\mathbf{y}}_{0} are −𝐌-\mathbf{M} and −h​𝐌-h\mathbf{M}, respectively. For each frame tt, the partial derivatives of 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t} with respect to the optimized initial configuration and velocity form the corresponding 𝐆t\mathbf{G}_{t}. We evaluate these derivatives at the converged state of frame tt and accumulate their contributions to the initial-state gradients using Equation (33).

For the velocity-reset approximation of quasi-static behavior, we set the predictor velocity to zero at every step, giving 𝐲^t=𝐲t−1+h2​𝐚t\widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{t}=\mathbf{y}_{t-1}+h^{2}\mathbf{a}_{t}. The mass-weighted quadratic term in Equation (6) remains, so each update still depends on the previous configuration. Differentiating its energy gradient with respect to 𝐲t−1\mathbf{y}_{t-1} contributes −𝐌-\mathbf{M} to 𝐂t,t−1\mathbf{C}_{t,t-1}. Substituting this contribution into Equation (32) gives the inertial contribution

(36) Δ​𝐛t−1(t),in=𝐌​𝝀t,t≥2.\Delta\mathbf{b}_{t-1}^{(t),\mathrm{in}}=\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t},\qquad t\geq 2.

4.5. Friction between frames

Friction adds a second source of temporal dependence: its energy uses both the current displacement and contact quantities computed from the previous configuration. DiffIPC differentiates this dependence for finite elements (Huang et al., 2024c). Here the point maps carry these history derivatives into the coupled FEM-affine recurrence, including contacts whose points use different motion representations. For contact cc, let 𝐠t,cfr,x\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x} be the friction energy gradient with respect to the current world-space point positions 𝐱tc\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}. The maps 𝐊t,c\mathbf{K}_{t,c} and 𝐊t−1,c\mathbf{K}_{t-1,c} relate the same contact points to the simulation DoFs at the two frames. With rest geometry fixed, these maps do not depend on the solved DoFs. Differentiating 𝐠t,cfr,y=𝐊t,c𝖳​𝐠t,cfr,x\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},y}=\mathbf{K}_{t,c}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x} with respect to 𝐲t−1\mathbf{y}_{t-1} therefore gives

(37) ∂𝐠t,cfr,y∂𝐲t−1=𝐊t,c𝖳​∂𝐠t,cfr,x∂𝐱t−1c​𝐊t−1,c.\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},y}}{\partial\mathbf{y}_{t-1}}=\mathbf{K}_{t,c}^{\mathsf{T}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}}{\partial\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{c}}\mathbf{K}_{t-1,c}.

This is the contact’s contribution to 𝐂t,t−1\mathbf{C}_{t,t-1}. For t≥2t\geq 2, contact cc contributes Δ​𝐛t−1(t,c),fr\Delta\mathbf{b}_{t-1}^{(t,c),\mathrm{fr}} to the earlier-frame right-hand side. Equation (32) gives

(38) Δ​𝐛t−1(t,c),fr=−𝐊t−1,c𝖳​(∂𝐠t,cfr,x∂𝐱t−1c)𝖳​𝐊t,c​𝝀t.\Delta\mathbf{b}_{t-1}^{(t,c),\mathrm{fr}}=-\mathbf{K}_{t-1,c}^{\mathsf{T}}\left(\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}}{\partial\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{c}}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{K}_{t,c}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t}.

Summing these per-contact vectors gives the friction part of Δ​𝐛t−1(t)\Delta\mathbf{b}_{t-1}^{(t)}. Each contact point retains its FEM or affine map, so the same expression covers contact between the two representations.

The relative tangential displacement is computed from the corresponding vertex displacements using closest-point interpolation weights and a tangent basis. These weights, the tangent basis, and the normal force are computed from the converged configuration of the previous frame. They remain fixed throughout the current frame’s solve. When differentiating with respect to the previous-frame positions, we also include the derivatives of these quantities. Appendix A.1 gives the friction law and its derivatives.

5. Affine-Body Derivatives for Shape, Initial States, and Control

The coupled adjoint describes how a loss responds to motion. To optimize an affine body’s shape or controls, we must also differentiate how those parameters enter the frame equations. In particular, an affine body can expose many rest-shape coordinates for design, while adding only twelve motion DoFs per solve. A rest-shape change affects mass and inertia, world-space contact geometry, and the maps from point-space forces to affine coordinates. Friction adds the dependence on that geometry at the previous frame.

We derive these parameter derivatives, followed by initial-state and joint-control derivatives. For a scalar parameter θk\theta_{k}, the partial derivative ∂𝐠t/∂θk\partial\mathbf{g}_{t}/\partial\theta_{k} forms column kk of 𝐆t\mathbf{G}_{t}, evaluated at fixed solved DoFs. The adjoint accounts for the resulting motion response, and Equation (30) combines −𝐆t𝖳​𝝀t-\mathbf{G}_{t}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t} with the explicit loss derivative ℓθ\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta}. The following derivatives preserve this separation, allowing surface design, placement, and control to share the twelve-DoF affine representation.

5.1. Rest-dependent mass and inertia

For affine body bb, let Ωb\Omega_{b} be its rest domain and ρb\rho_{b} its constant density. For a material point with rest position 𝐱¯\bar{\mathbf{x}}, the map 𝐉⁡(𝐱¯)\mathbf{J}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) in Equation (3) gives its world-space position as 𝐱t=𝐉⁡(𝐱¯)​𝐪t,b\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mathbf{J}(\bar{\mathbf{x}})\mathbf{q}_{t,b}. With rest geometry fixed, its velocity is 𝐱˙t=𝐉⁡(𝐱¯)​𝐪˙t,b\dot{\mathbf{x}}_{t}=\mathbf{J}(\bar{\mathbf{x}})\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{t,b}. The corresponding mass block is

(39) 𝐌b=∫Ωbρb​𝐉​(𝐱¯)𝖳​𝐉​(𝐱¯)​𝑑V.\mathbf{M}_{b}=\int_{\Omega_{b}}\rho_{b}\mathbf{J}(\bar{\mathbf{x}})^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{J}(\bar{\mathbf{x}})\,\mathrm{d}V.

Both 𝐌b\mathbf{M}_{b} and its shape derivative can be computed from the closed surface mesh. We express the volume integral as signed triangle contributions, each depending explicitly on the triangle’s rest vertices. Differentiating these expressions gives the mass-matrix derivatives directly from the design surface, without an interior tetrahedral discretization.

Expanding 𝐉​(𝐱¯)𝖳​𝐉​(𝐱¯)\mathbf{J}(\bar{\mathbf{x}})^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{J}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) in Equation (39) gives terms that are constant, linear, or quadratic in the rest position 𝐱¯\bar{\mathbf{x}}. The mass matrix 𝐌b\mathbf{M}_{b} is determined by three integrals over the body’s rest volume:

(40) mb\displaystyle m_{b} =∫Ωbρb​dV,\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega_{b}}\rho_{b}\,\mathrm{d}V,
𝐦b(1)\displaystyle\mathbf{m}_{b}^{(1)} =∫Ωbρb​𝐱¯​dV,\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega_{b}}\rho_{b}\bar{\mathbf{x}}\,\mathrm{d}V,
𝐐b(2)\displaystyle\mathbf{Q}_{b}^{(2)} =∫Ωbρb​𝐱¯​𝐱¯𝖳​dV.\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega_{b}}\rho_{b}\bar{\mathbf{x}}\bar{\mathbf{x}}^{\mathsf{T}}\,\mathrm{d}V.

Here mbm_{b} is the total mass. The vector 𝐦b(1)\mathbf{m}_{b}^{(1)} is the first mass moment and the matrix 𝐐b(2)\mathbf{Q}_{b}^{(2)} is the second mass moment. With density fixed, mbm_{b}, 𝐦b(1)\mathbf{m}_{b}^{(1)}, and 𝐐b(2)\mathbf{Q}_{b}^{(2)} depend only on the body’s rest shape.

The closed surface mesh provides these volume integrals. For an outward-oriented triangle ff with rest vertices 𝐱¯f,1\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{f,1}, 𝐱¯f,2\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{f,2}, and 𝐱¯f,3\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{f,3}, the three vertices and the origin define a signed tetrahedron. Its volume and mass-weighted integrals can be calculated directly from the three vertex positions. With 𝐬f=𝐱¯f,1+𝐱¯f,2+𝐱¯f,3\mathbf{s}_{f}=\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{f,1}+\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{f,2}+\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{f,3}, the signed contributions are

Vf\displaystyle V_{f} =16​𝐱¯f,1𝖳​(𝐱¯f,2×𝐱¯f,3),\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{6}\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{f,1}^{\mathsf{T}}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{f,2}\times\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{f,3}),
mf\displaystyle m_{f} =ρb​Vf,𝐦f(1)=mf4​𝐬f,\displaystyle=\rho_{b}V_{f},\qquad\mathbf{m}_{f}^{(1)}=\tfrac{m_{f}}{4}\mathbf{s}_{f},
(41) 𝐐f(2)\displaystyle\mathbf{Q}_{f}^{(2)} =mf20​(∑j=13𝐱¯f,j​𝐱¯f,j𝖳+𝐬f​𝐬f𝖳).\displaystyle=\tfrac{m_{f}}{20}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{3}\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{f,j}\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{f,j}^{\mathsf{T}}+\mathbf{s}_{f}\mathbf{s}_{f}^{\mathsf{T}}\right).

Summing mfm_{f}, 𝐦f(1)\mathbf{m}_{f}^{(1)}, and 𝐐f(2)\mathbf{Q}_{f}^{(2)} over all surface triangles gives mbm_{b}, 𝐦b(1)\mathbf{m}_{b}^{(1)}, and 𝐐b(2)\mathbf{Q}_{b}^{(2)}, respectively. Retaining the signs in these sums recovers the volume moments from the oriented surface triangles.

Using these quantities and the coordinate order in Equation (1), the affine-body mass matrix is

(42) 𝐌b=[mb​𝐈3𝐞1​(𝐦b(1))𝖳𝐞2​(𝐦b(1))𝖳𝐞3​(𝐦b(1))𝖳𝐦b(1)​𝐞1𝖳𝐐b(2)00𝐦b(1)​𝐞2𝖳0𝐐b(2)0𝐦b(1)​𝐞3𝖳00𝐐b(2)].\mathbf{M}_{b}=\begin{bmatrix}m_{b}\mathbf{I}_{3}&\mathbf{e}_{1}(\mathbf{m}_{b}^{(1)})^{\mathsf{T}}&\mathbf{e}_{2}(\mathbf{m}_{b}^{(1)})^{\mathsf{T}}&\mathbf{e}_{3}(\mathbf{m}_{b}^{(1)})^{\mathsf{T}}\\ \mathbf{m}_{b}^{(1)}\mathbf{e}_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}&\mathbf{Q}_{b}^{(2)}&0&0\\ \mathbf{m}_{b}^{(1)}\mathbf{e}_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}&0&\mathbf{Q}_{b}^{(2)}&0\\ \mathbf{m}_{b}^{(1)}\mathbf{e}_{3}^{\mathsf{T}}&0&0&\mathbf{Q}_{b}^{(2)}\end{bmatrix}.

The total mass determines the translation block. The first mass moment determines the blocks between translation and the affine transformation, while the second mass moment determines the blocks for the affine transformation.

Each contribution in Equation (41) is an explicit function of the triangle’s rest vertex positions. With density and mesh connectivity fixed, summing their derivatives over the surface triangles gives d​mb\mathrm{d}m_{b}, d​𝐦b(1)\mathrm{d}\mathbf{m}_{b}^{(1)}, and d​𝐐b(2)\mathrm{d}\mathbf{Q}_{b}^{(2)}. Substituting them into Equation (42) gives d​𝐌b\mathrm{d}\mathbf{M}_{b}. When the inverse mass matrix is needed, its derivative is d⁡(𝐌b−1)=−𝐌b−1​(d​𝐌b)​𝐌b−1\mathrm{d}(\mathbf{M}_{b}^{-1})=-\mathbf{M}_{b}^{-1}(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{M}_{b})\mathbf{M}_{b}^{-1}. Shape updates preserve the closed, consistently oriented, nondegenerate surface and the validity of its mass distribution. Invalid candidates are rejected before updating the simulation geometry.

5.2. Rest-shape gradients

Rest-shape derivatives express how the frame equations change when the affine design surface changes. Solved FEM positions and affine states are held fixed when forming 𝐆t\mathbf{G}_{t}, while an affine rest variation still moves its surface point by d​𝐱t,i=𝐀t,b​d​𝐱¯i\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{t,i}=\mathbf{A}_{t,b}\mathrm{d}\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i}. The resulting mass, contact-map, and energy-gradient variations are denoted by d​𝐌b\mathrm{d}\mathbf{M}_{b}, d​𝐊t,c\mathrm{d}\mathbf{K}_{t,c}, and d​𝐠t\mathrm{d}\mathbf{g}_{t}. They supply the corresponding parameter derivatives, with direct surface-loss dependence added separately to ℓθ\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta}.

Mass, inertia, and shape energy.

For body bb at frame tt, the inertial energy gradient is 𝐠t,bin=𝐌b​(𝐪t,b−𝐪^t,b)\mathbf{g}_{t,b}^{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbf{M}_{b}(\mathbf{q}_{t,b}-\widehat{\mathbf{q}}_{t,b}). The product rule gives the corresponding first-order change:

(43) d​𝐠t,bin=(d​𝐌b)​(𝐪t,b−𝐪^t,b)−𝐌b​d​𝐪^t,b.\mathrm{d}\mathbf{g}_{t,b}^{\mathrm{in}}=(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{M}_{b})(\mathbf{q}_{t,b}-\widehat{\mathbf{q}}_{t,b})-\mathbf{M}_{b}\,\mathrm{d}\widehat{\mathbf{q}}_{t,b}.

The first term uses the mass derivative derived above. The second includes any rest-shape dependence in the inputs to the predictor. The affine shape incremental potential is h2​κA​Vb​ψA​(𝐪t,b)h^{2}\kappa_{\mathrm{A}}V_{b}\psi_{\mathrm{A}}(\mathbf{q}_{t,b}), where κA\kappa_{\mathrm{A}} is the affine stiffness coefficient, VbV_{b} is the rest volume, and ψA\psi_{\mathrm{A}} is the near-rigidity penalty. Let 𝐠t,bshape\mathbf{g}_{t,b}^{\mathrm{shape}} be its gradient with respect to 𝐪t,b\mathbf{q}_{t,b}. With κA\kappa_{\mathrm{A}} and 𝐪t,b\mathbf{q}_{t,b} fixed, the rest-shape derivative of the combined inertial and shape contributions is

(44) d⁡(𝐠t,bin+𝐠t,bshape)\displaystyle\mathrm{d}(\mathbf{g}_{t,b}^{\mathrm{in}}+\mathbf{g}_{t,b}^{\mathrm{shape}}) =d​𝐠t,bin\displaystyle=\mathrm{d}\mathbf{g}_{t,b}^{\mathrm{in}}
+h2​κA​(d​Vb)​∇𝐪t,bψA.\displaystyle+h^{2}\kappa_{\mathrm{A}}(\mathrm{d}V_{b})\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{t,b}}\psi_{\mathrm{A}}.

The two contributions describe different physical effects of redesign: redistributing material changes the inertial response through 𝐌b\mathbf{M}_{b}, while changing the rest volume changes the scale of the near-rigidity energy. Both enter the parameter derivative at fixed affine coordinates. The adjoint then accounts for the resulting change in motion.

Collision-barrier derivatives and the point map.

For a surface vertex ii on body bb, partial differentiation with respect to 𝐱¯i\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i} holds the translation 𝐩t,b\mathbf{p}_{t,b} and affine transformation 𝐀t,b\mathbf{A}_{t,b} fixed. Equation (2) gives the resulting world-space position change as d​𝐱t,i=𝐀t,b​d​𝐱¯i\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{t,i}=\mathbf{A}_{t,b}\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i}. This variation also changes 𝐉i\mathbf{J}_{i} and the corresponding entries of the contact map 𝐊t,c\mathbf{K}_{t,c}. For contact cc, let d​𝐱tc\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c} collect the changes in its world-space point positions. Applying the product rule to the collision energy gradient 𝐠t,cct,y=𝐊t,c𝖳​𝐠t,cct,x\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{ct},y}=\mathbf{K}_{t,c}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{ct},x} gives its first-order change:

(45) d​𝐠t,cct,y\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{ct},y} =(d​𝐊t,c)𝖳​𝐠t,cct,x\displaystyle=(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{K}_{t,c})^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{ct},x}
+𝐊t,c𝖳​𝐇t,cct,x​d​𝐱tc.\displaystyle+\mathbf{K}_{t,c}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{H}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{ct},x}\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}.

Here ct\mathrm{ct} denotes the collision-barrier term, and 𝐇t,cct,x\mathbf{H}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{ct},x} is its Hessian with respect to the world-space point positions 𝐱tc\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}. The first term accounts for the changed mapping from a point force to the body’s affine equations: even an unchanged point-space force has a different contribution when its material point moves. The second term accounts for the force change caused by the altered world-space collision geometry. Rest-shape changes affect both the world-space collision gradient and the mapping 𝐊t,c\mathbf{K}_{t,c}, so both terms must be included. Varying only a selected scalar rest-coordinate θk\theta_{k}, while holding all other parameters and solved DoFs fixed, gives the corresponding partial derivative:

(46) ∂𝐠t,cct,y∂θk\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{ct},y}}{\partial\theta_{k}} =(∂𝐊t,c∂θk)𝖳​𝐠t,cct,x\displaystyle=\left(\frac{\partial\mathbf{K}_{t,c}}{\partial\theta_{k}}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{ct},x}
+𝐊t,c𝖳​𝐇t,cct,x​∂𝐱tc∂θk.\displaystyle+\mathbf{K}_{t,c}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{H}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{ct},x}\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}}{\partial\theta_{k}}.

∂𝐠t,cct,y/∂θk\partial\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{ct},y}/\partial\theta_{k} is contact cc’s collision contribution to column kk of 𝐆t\mathbf{G}_{t}.

Rest shape under frictional contact.

The friction energy at frame tt depends on the surface-point positions at both frames tt and t−1t-1. For vertex ii on affine body bb, these two positions are computed from the same rest position 𝐱¯i\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i} using Equation (2). We vary 𝐱¯i\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i} while keeping each frame’s translation and affine transformation at their converged values. The resulting world-space position changes are

d​𝐱t,i=𝐀t,b​d​𝐱¯i,d​𝐱t−1,i=𝐀t−1,b​d​𝐱¯i.\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{t,i}=\mathbf{A}_{t,b}\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i},\qquad\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{t-1,i}=\mathbf{A}_{t-1,b}\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i}.

A rest vertex identifies the same material point at both frames. Moving it can therefore change the relative sliding displacement even when the two affine transforms are held fixed. Its previous-frame position also determines the interpolation weights, contact-plane basis, and normal force used by the friction law. The shape derivative must include these changes together with the current point displacement.

Let 𝐇t,cfr,x=∂𝐠t,cfr,x/∂𝐱tc\mathbf{H}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}=\partial\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}/\partial\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c} and 𝐂t,cfr,x=∂𝐠t,cfr,x/∂𝐱t−1c\mathbf{C}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}=\partial\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}/\partial\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{c} be the derivatives with respect to the current and previous point positions. The block 𝐂t,cfr,x\mathbf{C}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x} includes the changes in the interpolation weights, tangent basis, and normal force. The rest-shape variation also changes 𝐊t,c\mathbf{K}_{t,c}. Applying the product rule to 𝐠t,cfr,y=𝐊t,c𝖳​𝐠t,cfr,x\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},y}=\mathbf{K}_{t,c}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x} therefore gives all three contributions:

(47) d​𝐠t,cfr,y\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},y} =(d​𝐊t,c)𝖳​𝐠t,cfr,x\displaystyle=(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{K}_{t,c})^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}
+𝐊t,c𝖳​𝐇t,cfr,x​d​𝐱tc\displaystyle+\mathbf{K}_{t,c}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{H}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}
+𝐊t,c𝖳​𝐂t,cfr,x​d​𝐱t−1c.\displaystyle+\mathbf{K}_{t,c}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{C}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{c}.

These terms capture the changed force map and the current- and previous-frame contact geometry at fixed simulated DoFs. Their contribution to 𝐆t\mathbf{G}_{t} complements the earlier-state dependence propagated by the history update in Section 4.5. Appendix A.1 provides the friction law in terms of contact-point positions and its derivatives.

Direct dependence of a surface loss.

A loss evaluated on an affine surface also depends on rest geometry through 𝐱t,i=𝐉i​𝐪t,b\mathbf{x}_{t,i}=\mathbf{J}_{i}\mathbf{q}_{t,b}. For a loss on surface positions at one frame tt, holding the simulation DoFs fixed gives the direct contribution

(48) ∇𝐱¯iL|𝐲t​fixed=𝐀t,b𝖳​∇𝐱t,iL.\left.\nabla_{\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i}}L\right|_{\mathbf{y}_{t}\ \mathrm{fixed}}=\mathbf{A}_{t,b}^{\mathsf{T}}\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t,i}}L.

For losses on several frames, these direct contributions are summed over the corresponding frames and included in ℓθ\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta}. They are added to the contributions through the frame equations in Equation (30). Garment Hanger (Figure 4) illustrates both contributions. Its support objective depends on the relative positions of the cloth straps and hanger shoulders. Changing the rest surface therefore affects the loss directly through the surface map and indirectly through the coupled motion, including frictional contact. Both contributions enter the rest-shape gradient.

5.3. Initial-state gradients

Following Section 4.4, we include the selected components of an affine body’s initial configuration 𝐪0,b\mathbf{q}_{0,b} and initial velocity 𝐪˙0,b\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{0,b} in 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}. Their parameter derivatives enter 𝐆t\mathbf{G}_{t} and determine the initial-state components of Δ​𝜽¯(t)\Delta\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(t)} in Equation (33). For these partial derivatives, the rest geometry, prescribed accelerations, and computed states 𝐲1,…,𝐲T\mathbf{y}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{y}_{T} remain unchanged. Only the selected initial values vary.

The first-frame inertial derivatives in Section 4.4 use the mass block 𝐌b\mathbf{M}_{b} for affine body bb:

(49) ∂𝐠1,bin∂𝐪0,b=−𝐌b,∂𝐠1,bin∂𝐪˙0,b=−h​𝐌b.\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}_{1,b}^{\mathrm{in}}}{\partial\mathbf{q}_{0,b}}=-\mathbf{M}_{b},\qquad\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}_{1,b}^{\mathrm{in}}}{\partial\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{0,b}}=-h\mathbf{M}_{b}.

The initial configuration also appears in the second-frame BDF1 predictor, 𝐪^2,b=2​𝐪1,b−𝐪0,b+h2​𝐚2,b\widehat{\mathbf{q}}_{2,b}=2\mathbf{q}_{1,b}-\mathbf{q}_{0,b}+h^{2}\mathbf{a}_{2,b}. Differentiating 𝐠2,bin=𝐌b​(𝐪2,b−𝐪^2,b)\mathbf{g}_{2,b}^{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbf{M}_{b}(\mathbf{q}_{2,b}-\widehat{\mathbf{q}}_{2,b}) with respect to 𝐪0,b\mathbf{q}_{0,b} gives

(50) ∂𝐠2,bin∂𝐪0,b=𝐌b.\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}_{2,b}^{\mathrm{in}}}{\partial\mathbf{q}_{0,b}}=\mathbf{M}_{b}.

The first-frame derivatives contribute to 𝐆1\mathbf{G}_{1}, and the second-frame derivative contributes to 𝐆2\mathbf{G}_{2}. Let 𝝀t,b\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t,b} contain the twelve entries of the coupled adjoint 𝝀t\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t} corresponding to body bb. Substituting these derivatives into Equation (33) gives the inertial contributions to the initial-state gradients:

(51) Δ​𝐪¯0,b\displaystyle\Delta\bar{\mathbf{q}}_{0,b} =𝐌b​𝝀1,b−𝐌b​𝝀2,b,\displaystyle=\mathbf{M}_{b}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{1,b}-\mathbf{M}_{b}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{2,b},
Δ​𝐪˙¯0,b\displaystyle\Delta\overline{\dot{\mathbf{q}}}_{0,b} =h​𝐌b​𝝀1,b.\displaystyle=h\mathbf{M}_{b}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{1,b}.

For a one-frame trajectory, the term containing 𝝀2,b\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{2,b} is omitted.

Friction provides an additional initial-configuration derivative. At the first frame, its previous-frame positions are the initial surface positions 𝐱0,i=𝐉i​𝐪0,b\mathbf{x}_{0,i}=\mathbf{J}_{i}\mathbf{q}_{0,b}. Changing 𝐪0,b\mathbf{q}_{0,b} changes these positions and the interpolation weights, tangent basis, and normal force computed from them. We compute this derivative using Equation (37) with t=1t=1. Since 𝐪0,b\mathbf{q}_{0,b} is an input parameter, this derivative contributes to 𝐆1\mathbf{G}_{1} and the parameter-gradient update, rather than an earlier-frame vector 𝐛0\mathbf{b}_{0}.

For the velocity-reset updates used to approximate quasi-static behavior in Section 4.4, the first-frame predictor is 𝐪^1,b=𝐪0,b+h2​𝐚1,b\widehat{\mathbf{q}}_{1,b}=\mathbf{q}_{0,b}+h^{2}\mathbf{a}_{1,b}. Its inertial derivatives are −𝐌b-\mathbf{M}_{b} with respect to 𝐪0,b\mathbf{q}_{0,b} and zero with respect to 𝐪˙0,b\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{0,b}. Subsequent predictors use the previous solved configuration without an explicit 𝐪0,b\mathbf{q}_{0,b} term. In this mode, the inertial contributions are Δ​𝐪¯0,b=𝐌b​𝝀1,b{\Delta\bar{\mathbf{q}}_{0,b}=\mathbf{M}_{b}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{1,b}} and Δ​𝐪˙¯0,b=𝟎{\Delta\overline{\dot{\mathbf{q}}}_{0,b}=\mathbf{0}}. The first-frame friction contribution is included as described above.

5.4. Joint targets and forces

Revolute and prismatic joint targets and forces provide actuation parameters alongside rest shapes and initial states. Their reference geometry and driving stiffness remain fixed during control optimization. Let uj,tu_{j,t} denote the scalar target, force, or torque applied to joint jj at frame tt, and let 𝐠t,jjoint\mathbf{g}_{t,j}^{\mathrm{joint}} denote its contribution to the frame energy gradient. Equation (33) gives this joint’s contribution Δ​u¯j,t\Delta\bar{u}_{j,t} to the control gradient:

(52) Δ​u¯j,t=−(∂𝐠t,jjoint∂uj,t)𝖳​𝝀t.\Delta\bar{u}_{j,t}=-\left(\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}_{t,j}^{\mathrm{joint}}}{\partial u_{j,t}}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t}.

Although the local control derivative involves only the two joint-connected bodies, its product with the coupled adjoint includes their response through contact with the rest of the scene. Joint targets and forces can therefore be optimized for objectives on interacting objects, using the same backward system as shape and initial-state parameters.

Actuation energies and parameter derivatives.

For the local formulas, we omit the joint and frame indices. Let aa be the applied target, ff the joint force (a linear force for a prismatic joint and a torque for a revolute joint), and kk the effective driving stiffness. The affine DoFs of the two bodies connected by the joint are denoted by 𝐪p\mathbf{q}_{p} and 𝐪c\mathbf{q}_{c}. The vector 𝐪=[𝐪p𝖳,𝐪c𝖳]𝖳\mathbf{q}=[\mathbf{q}_{p}^{\mathsf{T}},\mathbf{q}_{c}^{\mathsf{T}}]^{\mathsf{T}} collects both bodies’ DoFs, with ∇=∇𝐪\nabla=\nabla_{\mathbf{q}}. For a prismatic joint, let ξ\xi denote the relative displacement between the two joint attachment points, projected onto the joint axis of body cc in world space. Its energy and control derivatives are

Φpri\displaystyle\Phi^{\mathrm{pri}} =12​k​(ξ−a)2−f​ξ,\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}k(\xi-a)^{2}-f\xi,
𝐠pri\displaystyle\mathbf{g}^{\mathrm{pri}} =∇Φpri=[k(ξ−a)−f]∇ξ,\displaystyle=\nabla\Phi^{\mathrm{pri}}=[k(\xi-a)-f]\nabla\xi,
(53) ∂𝐠pri∂a\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}^{\mathrm{pri}}}{\partial a} =−k∇ξ,∂𝐠pri∂f=−∇ξ.\displaystyle=-k\nabla\xi,\qquad\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}^{\mathrm{pri}}}{\partial f}=-\nabla\xi.

The gradient ∇ξ\nabla\xi also accounts for how the world-space joint axis of body cc changes with 𝐪c\mathbf{q}_{c}. The quadratic term penalizes displacement away from the target aa, whereas −f​ξ-f\xi specifies the applied joint force along the joint coordinate. Targets and joint forces therefore enter the same frame equation through different parameter derivatives.

For a revolute joint, two scalar quantities srs_{\mathrm{r}} and crc_{\mathrm{r}} computed from the bodies’ transformed reference directions define the relative angle α=atan2⁡(sr,cr)\alpha=\operatorname{atan2}(s_{\mathrm{r}},c_{\mathrm{r}}). For target aa, define

(54) Sr=sr​cos⁡a−cr​sin⁡a,Cr=cr​cos⁡a+sr​sin⁡a.S_{\mathrm{r}}=s_{\mathrm{r}}\cos a-c_{\mathrm{r}}\sin a,\qquad C_{\mathrm{r}}=c_{\mathrm{r}}\cos a+s_{\mathrm{r}}\sin a.

These quantities compare the relative orientation with the target. For rigid rotations with orthonormal reference directions and aligned joint axes, they reduce to Sr=sin⁡(α−a)S_{\mathrm{r}}=\sin(\alpha-a) and Cr=cos⁡(α−a)C_{\mathrm{r}}=\cos(\alpha-a). The squared sine vanishes both at the target and a half-turn away. The cosine term below gives the half-turn a positive penalty. The periodic target energy is

Φrev\displaystyle\Phi^{\mathrm{rev}} =12​k​[Sr2+wc​(1−Cr)2]−f​α,\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}k\bigl[S_{\mathrm{r}}^{2}+w_{c}(1-C_{\mathrm{r}})^{2}\bigr]-f\alpha,
𝐠rev\displaystyle\mathbf{g}^{\mathrm{rev}} =∇Φrev\displaystyle=\nabla\Phi^{\mathrm{rev}}
(55) =k[Sr∇Sr−wc(1−Cr)∇Cr]−f∇α.\displaystyle=k\bigl[S_{\mathrm{r}}\nabla S_{\mathrm{r}}-w_{c}(1-C_{\mathrm{r}})\nabla C_{\mathrm{r}}\bigr]-f\nabla\alpha.

Here wc=0.02w_{c}=0.02 is the fixed relative weight of the cosine penalty, not an optimized control. The joint energy uses srs_{\mathrm{r}} and crc_{\mathrm{r}} computed directly from the affine-transformed joint reference directions. Their derivatives account for changes in both the lengths and orientations of these directions. The angle derivatives used by the torque term −f​α-f\alpha are given in Appendix A.3.

The partial derivatives with respect to the applied target and joint force are

(56) ∂𝐠rev∂a\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\partial a} =k[(−Cr−wc(1−Cr))∇Sr\displaystyle=k\bigl[(-C_{\mathrm{r}}-w_{c}(1-C_{\mathrm{r}}))\nabla S_{\mathrm{r}}
+(wc−1)Sr∇Cr],\displaystyle+(w_{c}-1)S_{\mathrm{r}}\nabla C_{\mathrm{r}}\bigr],
∂𝐠rev∂f\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\partial f} =−∇α.\displaystyle=-\nabla\alpha.

All control derivatives are evaluated at the converged frame states. At fixed control values, differentiating the state gradients gives the full joint Hessians ∇2Φpri\nabla^{2}\Phi^{\mathrm{pri}} and ∇2Φrev\nabla^{2}\Phi^{\mathrm{rev}}. These include the second derivatives of the joint coordinates and of the potential terms linear in the joint force. Appendix A.3 gives the geometric definitions of ξ\xi, srs_{\mathrm{r}}, and crc_{\mathrm{r}}, their first and second coordinate derivatives, and the full Hessians in Equation (91).

6. GPU Backward and Reusable Interface

Compact coordinates and GPU parallelism reduce different parts of the backward cost. The coupled adjoint solve captures interactions across the scene, while local derivative products expose parallel work over elements, surface triangles, contacts, and joints. Conditional CUDA Graphs reduce repeated CPU coordination during the solve, and parallel accumulation returns gradients to earlier states and physical parameters (Figure 5). A PyTorch interface makes this computation reusable across task-specific designs and objectives.

The adjoint system is assembled from each frame’s converged FEM and affine states. Equation (2) recovers the affine surface positions. The backward pass evaluates contact derivatives using the same contact pairs and distance formulas as the forward solve at this converged state. Previous-frame friction weights, contact-plane bases, and normal forces retain the history dependence derived in Section 4.5. StiffGIPC’s parallel global Hessian assembly (Huang et al., 2025a) combines element, body, collision, friction, and joint contributions, including FEM-affine cross terms. The resulting Hessian is assembled once per reverse frame and remains fixed throughout its PCG solve, avoiding a repeat of the nonlinear forward iterations.

6.1. PCG with conditional CUDA Graphs

The adjoint in Equation (31) uses the same frame Hessian as the converged forward equations, allowing StiffGIPC’s highly parallel GPU PCG solver (Huang et al., 2025a) to serve both forward and backward computations. Compact affine coordinates reduce PCG’s numerical workload, making repeated CPU kernel launches and convergence synchronization a larger fraction of solve time. The stricter backward residual tolerance can amplify this cost over more iterations. To address this, we build a PCG pipeline managed by a conditional CUDA Graph, based on the PCG recurrence kernels (Baraff and Witkin, 1998), their execution dependencies, and the convergence checks (Figure 5). Once launched from the CPU, the graph initializes PCG and then repeats its iterations and convergence checks entirely on the GPU until convergence or the iteration limit is reached, eliminating per-iteration kernel launches and CPU–GPU synchronization.

For each reverse frame, we solve the assembled adjoint system using a reusable CUDA Graph (Algorithm 2). Its inputs 𝐇t\mathbf{H}_{t}, 𝐛t\mathbf{b}_{t}, and preconditioner 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t} are updated between frames and stay fixed during each solve. The graph preserves the dependencies between PCG kernels, while GPU convergence checks govern its conditional loop, so the same graph can run a different number of iterations. It can still be reused when contact sets change, as long as the kernel configuration and storage stay compatible. This reuse spreads graph construction across frames and removes per-iteration CPU coordination, so compact FEM-affine adjoint systems can benefit from their reduced numerical workload. The GPU convergence check compares the preconditioned residual measure |χ(k)|=|(𝐫(k))𝖳​𝒫t−1​𝐫(k)||\chi^{(k)}|=|(\mathbf{r}^{(k)})^{\mathsf{T}}\mathcal{P}_{t}^{-1}\mathbf{r}^{(k)}| with the target χtol=ηcg​|χ(0)|\chi_{\mathrm{tol}}=\eta_{\mathrm{cg}}|\chi^{(0)}|, set at the start of each solve. The conditional loop stops when this target is reached or the iteration count reaches kmaxk_{\max}. The default backward settings are ηcg=10−14\eta_{\mathrm{cg}}=10^{-14} and kmax=3×104k_{\max}=3\times 10^{4}. Only an adjoint whose final residual measure meets the target is accepted for the gradient accumulation described next.

6.2. GPU-parallel gradient accumulation

The parameter-gradient and earlier-frame contributions in Equations (33) and (32) share the coupled adjoint 𝝀t\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t}. Its entries contain the influence of interactions across the scene, but each derivative product accesses the DoFs of a local element, contact and joint. Surface triangles provide the local mass and volume derivatives for affine shape design. This locality exposes parallel work even when a body has a compact motion state.

The parameter-gradient update is organized as parallel GPU tasks over FEM elements, contact pairs, joints, and affine surface triangles. Each task computes one local contribution to the gradient of a selected parameter. For affine rest-shape gradients, tasks assigned to individual surface triangles compute the mass-matrix and volume derivative contributions. Each task reads only the adjoint entries for the DoFs involved and evaluates their inner product with the corresponding parameter derivative. With the frame adjoint 𝝀t\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t} solved, the local derivative products are independent and evaluated in parallel. Atomic additions combine contributions to the same parameter-gradient entry. Let 𝐠t[ι]\mathbf{g}_{t}^{[\iota]} denote a local contribution to 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t}. The total loss gradient for parameter θk\theta_{k} is

(57) θ¯k=(ℓθ)k−∑t=1T∑ι(∂𝐠t[ι]∂θk)𝖳​𝝀t[ι].\bar{\theta}_{k}=(\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta})_{k}-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{\iota}\left(\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}_{t}^{[\iota]}}{\partial\theta_{k}}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t}^{[\iota]}.

Here (ℓθ)k(\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta})_{k} is the direct loss derivative with all solved states fixed. This decomposition sums the frame contributions in Equation (33) without assembling the global parameter-derivative matrix 𝐆t\mathbf{G}_{t}. The required derivatives come from Section 5, including inertia in Equation (43), initial states in Equations (49)–(50), and joint controls in Equation (52). Material derivatives are given in Appendix A.2.

Friction follows the same decomposition. The mapped adjoint 𝐊t,i​𝝀t\mathbf{K}_{t,i}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t} is computed once per vertex and reused by all contacts involving that vertex. For each contact, a separate GPU task computes one entry of

𝜸t,c=(∂𝐠t,cfr,x∂𝐱t−1c)𝖳​𝐊t,c​𝝀t,\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{t,c}=\left(\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}}{\partial\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{c}}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{K}_{t,c}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t},

without assembling the contact derivative matrix. Entries are summed at mesh vertices, and the resulting sum is mapped to previous-frame DoFs (Equation (38)). Contacts sharing a vertex therefore apply 𝐊t−1,i𝖳\mathbf{K}_{t-1,i}^{\mathsf{T}} only once. For a free FEM vertex ii, −𝜸ti-\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{t}^{i} is accumulated directly into the corresponding entries of 𝐛t−1\mathbf{b}_{t-1}. For affine bodies, the contributions −𝐊t−1,i𝖳​𝜸ti-\mathbf{K}_{t-1,i}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{t}^{i} are summed over their vertices into the body’s twelve entries in 𝐛t−1\mathbf{b}_{t-1}. The per-vertex vectors 𝜸ti\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{t}^{i} are also reused for the rest-shape gradient contribution arising from previous-frame contact positions (Equation (47)). Motion changes propagate through the earlier-frame right-hand sides, and the remaining rest-shape terms reuse the point gradients and Hessians assembled before affine conversion, without adding motion DoFs.

The inertial history terms in Equations (35)–(36) are likewise evaluated independently across vertices and bodies. All contributions to an earlier right-hand side must be accumulated before its adjoint solve. Parallelism therefore lies within each reverse frame, while frames follow the dependency order in Section 4.3. For a fixed trajectory and scalar loss, all selected parameters share the same frame adjoint, so adding parameters requires local derivative computation rather than additional coupled solves.

6.3. A reusable interface for inverse problems

The parameter map converts user-defined design variables into physical parameters such as rest geometry, material properties, or joint controls. The output map converts simulated DoFs into quantities used to evaluate the loss, such as surface vertex positions. PyTorch differentiates both maps and the loss, while DiffGIPC computes derivatives through the coupled simulation. A loss evaluated on one object can therefore guide the optimization of another object’s parameters through their physical interactions.

Let 𝐳∈ℝnz\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{z}} contain the optimizer variables, ϕ\phi map them to physical parameters 𝜽∈ℝnθ\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\theta}}, and 𝒪\mathcal{O} form the quantities used by the scalar loss ℓ\ell from the converged states:

(58) 𝜽\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\theta} =ϕ⁡(𝐳),\displaystyle=\phi(\mathbf{z}),
𝐨\displaystyle\mathbf{o} =𝒪⁡(𝐲1,…,𝐲T,𝜽),\displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(\mathbf{y}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{y}_{T},\boldsymbol{\theta}),
L\displaystyle L =ℓ⁡(𝐨,𝜽).\displaystyle=\ell(\mathbf{o},\boldsymbol{\theta}).

The parameter map imposes task-specific constraints or shares design variables across physical parameters, so nzn_{z} need not equal nθn_{\theta}. The output map combines quantities from different objects and frames without changing the coordinates of the coupled solve.

PyTorch differentiates the loss and output map to obtain

(59) ℓo=∇𝐨ℓ,ℓt=(∂𝒪∂𝐲t)𝖳​ℓo.\boldsymbol{\ell}_{o}=\nabla_{\mathbf{o}}\ell,\qquad\boldsymbol{\ell}_{t}=\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{O}}{\partial\mathbf{y}_{t}}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\ell}_{o}.

For affine surface points, 𝐉i𝖳\mathbf{J}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}} maps point gradients to body DoFs as in Equation (18), whereas FEM positions use the identity map. Selecting outputs sets the direct loss gradients, not the dependencies retained by the adjoint. A frame absent from 𝒪\mathcal{O} has ℓt=𝟎\boldsymbol{\ell}_{t}=\mathbf{0} but can still receive contributions from later frames. The output map and loss may also depend explicitly on physical parameters. With the simulated DoFs fixed, their contribution is

(60) ℓθ=∇𝜽ℓ|𝐨​fixed+(∂𝒪∂𝜽)𝖳​ℓo.\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta}=\left.\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell\right|_{\mathbf{o}\ \mathrm{fixed}}+\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{O}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\ell}_{o}.

For example, changing an affine rest surface moves its world-space points even at fixed motion DoFs. This explicit geometric effect is distinct from the change in simulated motion accounted for by the adjoint. The vectors ℓt\boldsymbol{\ell}_{t} and ℓθ\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta} initialize the right-hand sides and parameter gradient in Section 4.3. The GPU backward pass then supplies the physical gradient, which PyTorch maps to the optimizer variables:

(61) 𝜽¯\displaystyle\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}} =ℓθ−∑t=1T𝐆t𝖳​𝝀t,\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\theta}-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf{G}_{t}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t},
∇𝐳L\displaystyle\nabla_{\mathbf{z}}L =(∂ϕ∂𝐳)𝖳​𝜽¯.\displaystyle=\left(\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial\mathbf{z}}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}.

Task parameterizations and objectives can therefore change without changing the coupled backward equations. In Garment Hanger (Figure 4), two shared shoulder-control scales specify the rest surface, while the loss measures support using both hanger and cloth positions. PyTorch differentiates the shape parameterization and geometric loss. DiffGIPC combines the direct surface dependence with the gradient through their coupled motion, retaining twelve motion DoFs for the hanger. The same composition applies to the physical parameter families listed in Table 7 (Appendix B). Additional physical models enter through their local derivatives, preserving the distinction between task design and coupled simulation.

7. Evaluation

Our evaluation examines the parameter-to-output dependencies supported by DiffGIPC and the cost of forward and backward evaluations across full-space and affine motion representations. The shared full-space FEM benchmarks from DiffIPC (Huang et al., 2024c) cover initial motion, rest design, and material or friction fitting at their original low mesh resolutions. In these benchmarks, both methods use full-space FEM. Further experiments exercise cloth design, affine shape and placement, and articulated control, including mixed-coordinate inverse problems. We first compare optimization outcomes and evaluation times on the shared FEM benchmarks, then demonstrate the coupled design and control tasks. Gradient validation assesses agreement between analytic gradients and finite differences, while studies of motion representation, resolution, and GPU execution explain the optimization cost.

For the shared benchmarks, DiffGIPC runs on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 and DiffIPC on an Intel Core i9-13900K. Both use double-precision arithmetic and the same convergence tolerances. Appendix B summarizes the simulation settings in Table 6 and the differentiated parameter families in Table 7. A forward evaluation simulates a trajectory to the task’s observation horizon. A backward evaluation computes its loss gradient over that trajectory. NfwdN_{\mathrm{fwd}} counts forward evaluations, including line-search trials and verification runs, while NbwdN_{\mathrm{bwd}} counts complete gradient evaluations used for optimization. Let t¯f\bar{t}_{f} and t¯b\bar{t}_{b} denote their mean times. The combined mean time is t¯f+b=t¯f+t¯b\bar{t}_{f+b}=\bar{t}_{f}+\bar{t}_{b}. The accumulated evaluation time is Teval=Nfwd​t¯f+Nbwd​t¯bT_{\mathrm{eval}}={N_{\mathrm{fwd}}}\bar{t}_{f}+{N_{\mathrm{bwd}}}\bar{t}_{b}. In the loss definitions below, 𝐱t,i\mathbf{x}_{t,i} is the world-space position of vertex ii at observation frame tt, and a star denotes a prescribed target held fixed during optimization. Each task specifies its observation endpoint TT or selected frame set. Unsubscripted norms are Euclidean norms, and ∥⋅∥F\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{F}} denotes the Frobenius norm for matrices.

7.1. Comparison with DiffIPC

The shared FEM benchmarks establish the framework’s coverage in full-space FEM before introducing affine design and control. They progress from contact-driven motion to rest-shape design and parameter fitting, changing both the optimized input and the observed response. Figure 11 compares their optimization histories, and Table 1 reports the corresponding evaluation times. We relate each task’s objective to its physical outcome before examining the computational cost.

Bunny collision.

We optimize a shared initial velocity for the vertices of one bunny so that collision moves the other bunny to a target. The objective uses only the second bunny’s volume-weighted horizontal center after 40 frames:

(62) Lbunny=‖𝐜x​z​(𝐱T(2))−𝐜x​z∗‖2.L_{\mathrm{bunny}}=\|\mathbf{c}_{xz}(\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(2)})-\mathbf{c}_{xz}^{*}\|^{2}.

Here 𝐜x​z\mathbf{c}_{xz} is the volume-weighted horizontal (x,z)(x,z) center of the second bunny and T=40T=40. Because the loss observes only that body, the optimized velocity affects it through collision. Figure 6 shows the final position approaching the target. Section 7.4 revisits this task across motion representations.

Tentacle trajectory matching.
