The first deformable body’s shared initial velocity is optimized while the second body’s initial velocity remains fixed. Let 𝐜ttent\mathbf{c}_{t}^{\mathrm{tent}} be the first body’s volume-weighted position, using fixed rest-tetrahedron weights. Its trajectory-matching objective is

(63) Ltentacle=200​h​∑t=1T‖𝐜ttent−𝐜ttent,∗‖2,L_{\mathrm{tentacle}}=200h\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|\mathbf{c}_{t}^{\mathrm{tent}}-\mathbf{c}_{t}^{\mathrm{tent},*}\|^{2},

where T=100T=100 and 𝐜ttent,∗\mathbf{c}_{t}^{\mathrm{tent},*} is the prescribed target. Thus observations throughout the trajectory contribute to the initial-velocity gradient through motion and friction history; Figure 7 shows the endpoint.

Loaded Support design.

Selected rest vertices of a FEM support are optimized under downward loading, with its supports fixed. At the end of each 20-frame simulation, the squared-stress term is Lstress=10−8​∑e∈𝒯dVe​‖𝐏e‖F2L_{\mathrm{stress}}=10^{-8}\sum_{e\in{\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{d}}}}V_{e}\|{{\mathbf{P}}_{e}}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}. Here 𝒯d\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{d}} is the evaluated tetrahedron set, VeV_{e} is the rest volume, and 𝐏e\mathbf{P}_{e} is the first Piola stress evaluated at T=20T=20. Rest-volume weighting makes larger stressed regions contribute proportionally more. A surface-smoothing penalty discourages local irregularities in the designed rest geometry. The optimized loss is Lsupport=Lstress+LsmL_{\mathrm{support}}=L_{\mathrm{stress}}+L_{\mathrm{sm}}. The smoothing set 𝒱sm\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{sm}} contains surface vertices selected in rest coordinates. For each i∈𝒱smi\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{sm}}, let 𝒩sm​(i)\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{sm}}(i) be its surface-edge neighbors that also belong to 𝒱sm\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{sm}}. Using the current rest positions 𝐱¯i\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i}, the penalty is

(64) Lsm=∑i∈𝒱sm‖∑j∈𝒩sm​(i)(𝐱¯i−𝐱¯j)∑j∈𝒩sm​(i)‖𝐱¯i−𝐱¯j‖‖2.L_{\mathrm{sm}}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{sm}}}\left\|\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{sm}}(i)}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{j})}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{sm}}(i)}\|\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\|}\right\|^{2}.

Vertices without neighbors in this set contribute zero. This term measures each selected vertex’s deviation from its neighbors’ mean position, normalized by the mean incident edge length. Figure 8 shows how the redesigned geometry redistributes stress under the same loading and color scale. The loss histories in Figure 11 reach similar final objective levels for both methods. Their intermediate jumps occur when remeshing changes the stress discretization. Gradients are evaluated on each current fixed mesh, with feasible rest-shape updates selected by backtracking. The task demonstrates rest-shape design through the combined changes in geometry, element volume, and elastic response.

Material identification.

A homogeneous FEM cube is compressed by prescribed displacements on its two opposing faces. Its material response is fitted to a fixed reference deformation using surface-vertex positions. Two shared logarithmic variables, zvol=log⁡λLam​e´z_{\mathrm{vol}}=\log\lambda_{\mathrm{Lam\acute{e}}} and zstretch=log⁡μLam​e´z_{\mathrm{stretch}}=\log\mu_{\mathrm{Lam\acute{e}}}, parameterize the positive Lamé inputs λLam​e´\lambda_{\mathrm{Lam\acute{e}}} and μLam​e´\mu_{\mathrm{Lam\acute{e}}}. They determine the deformation coefficients of the stable Neo-Hookean energy as

(65) λ=ezvol+ezstretch,μ=ezstretch.\lambda=e^{z_{\mathrm{vol}}}+e^{z_{\mathrm{stretch}}},\qquad\mu=e^{z_{\mathrm{stretch}}}.

The same coefficient pair is assigned to every tetrahedron. The loss is Lmat=5×104∑i∈ℳ∥𝐱T,i−𝐱i∗∥2L_{\mathrm{mat}}=5\times 10^{4}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}\|\mathbf{x}_{T,i}-\mathbf{x}_{i}^{*}\|^{2}. Here ℳ\mathcal{M} contains prescribed vertex markers on the cube’s face in the rest configuration. The marker indices remain unchanged during optimization, so 𝐱T,i\mathbf{x}_{T,i} and 𝐱i∗\mathbf{x}_{i}^{*} refer to the simulated and reference positions of the same vertex, not to a nearest-point match. The factor 5×1045\times 10^{4} sets the numerical scale of the squared-position loss, which is summed rather than averaged over the markers. The timing configuration uses T=10T=10 simulation steps with h=0.1h=0.1 s, and the loss is evaluated only at the final step. Both Lamé input parameters are initialized to 4×1054\times 10^{5}. Both methods reach similar marker-position errors at the plotted scale. Figure 9 shows the separately rendered frame-19 configurations approaching the reference deformation. This task demonstrates fitting a shared material response from surface-position errors through the positive coefficient map.

Friction optimization.

The bunny-slide friction coefficient is fitted to a target position at frame 100, with h=0.02h=0.02 s. The loss is Lfr=100​(cz​(𝐱T)−zend)2L_{\mathrm{fr}}={100}(c_{z}(\mathbf{x}_{T})-z_{\mathrm{end}})^{2}, where czc_{z} is the bunny’s volume-weighted center coordinate, zendz_{\mathrm{end}} is the slide endpoint, and T=100T=100. The coefficient changes from 0.50.5 to 0.10.1 (Table 6 in Appendix B). Figure 10 shows the corresponding change in sliding distance at the fixed observation time. This task isolates the coefficient-to-motion dependence: geometry and initial motion remain fixed, and the optimized friction changes the cumulative sliding response.

Together, the shared benchmarks test gradients through collision-transmitted motion, observations over time, loaded shape changes, material fitting and friction response. Table 1 measures the cost of that optimization capability with full-space FEM in both systems. The complete backward pass is 12.312.3–34.1×34.1\times faster, including Hessian assembly, the adjoint solve, and gradient accumulation. Combined forward and backward speedups range from 10.6×10.6\times for friction fitting to 60.9×60.9\times for material fitting, while forward speedups are 10.510.5–88.1×88.1\times. These gains demonstrate efficient trajectory-gradient evaluation before introducing affine motion reduction. Section 7.4 examines that additional benefit, and Section 7.5 relates evaluation cost to complete optimization workloads.

7.2. Rest-shape design and stable placement

The design tasks separate the object being changed from the quantities used to judge the result. Cloth fitting maps a size parameter to a deforming garment, hanger design optimizes an affine surface through its effect on supported cloth, and stone placement adjusts initial positions while preserving shape. Together they demonstrate how rest geometry and initial-state parameters act through the same coupled trajectory gradient.

Cloth rest-scale fitting.

A single optimizer variable scales the garment’s rest shape, with a fixed mannequin. This map changes many rest coordinates while preserving full-space cloth deformation. At the observation endpoint T=48T=48, the target drape defines Lcloth=∑i∈𝒱cloth‖𝐱T,i−𝐱i∗‖2L_{\mathrm{cloth}}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{cloth}}}\|\mathbf{x}_{T,i}-\mathbf{x}_{i}^{*}\|^{2}, where 𝒱cloth\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{cloth}} contains all garment vertices and 𝐱i∗\mathbf{x}_{i}^{*} is the fixed target position of the corresponding material vertex. After 5 updates, the optimized drape approaches the target in Figure 12. The result demonstrates how a low-dimensional design parameter controls detailed simulated geometry through rest-shape derivatives.

Garment Hanger shoulder design.

Each shoulder profile is controlled by a quadratic Bézier curve with two fixed endpoints and one movable middle control point. The design variables sxs_{x} and sys_{y} adjust the middle control point’s horizontal and vertical positions. Starting from (sx,sy)=(1,1)(s_{x},s_{y})=(1,1), decreasing sxs_{x} moves the point toward the hanger’s centerline, and decreasing sys_{y} lowers it. The reflected curve uses the same pair, so both shoulders change symmetrically without moving their endpoints. The affine hanger retains twelve motion DoFs and supports a garment with friction coefficient 0.050.05.

At the terminal frame, RstipR_{s}^{\mathrm{tip}} and RsstrapR_{s}^{\mathrm{strap}} denote the horizontal positions of the hanger’s shoulder tip and the corresponding strap’s outer edge, respectively, on the left or right side s∈{L,R}s\in\{\mathrm{L},\mathrm{R}\}. On each side, horizontal coordinates increase from the hanger’s centerline toward the shoulder tip. Their difference therefore measures how far the hanger extends beyond the strap. The quantity dsd_{s} is the minimum three-dimensional distance between the selected strap and corresponding upper-shoulder vertices. For the fixed target margin δ=0.205\delta=0.205 m, the support margin and loss are

ms\displaystyle m_{s} =Rstip−Rsstrap−max⁡(ds−0.01,0),\displaystyle=R_{s}^{\mathrm{tip}}-R_{s}^{\mathrm{strap}}-\max(d_{s}-0.01,0),
Lhanger\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{hanger}} =104​∑s∈{L,R}max⁡(δ−ms,0)2.\displaystyle=10^{4}\sum_{s\in\{\mathrm{L},\mathrm{R}\}}\max(\delta-m_{s},0)^{2}.

The gap penalty reduces the margin when the strap separates from the shoulder by more than 0.010.01 m. Both surfaces contribute to the loss, whose shape gradient includes direct geometric and coupled-motion contributions (Section 5.2).

Each optimization rollout ends at the first margin violation ms<δm_{s}<\delta after the corresponding strap approaches within 0.010.01 m of its shoulder, or at frame 600. The optimized control-point scales (sx,sy)=(0.8285,0.8000)(s_{x},s_{y})=(0.8285,0.8000) move the middle control points inward and downward. The resulting hanger retains both straps in two independent 600-frame checks (Figure 4). After each strap contacts the hanger, its support margin must remain nonnegative (ms≥0m_{s}\geq 0) until frame 600. The larger target margin δ\delta is used to guide optimization. Figure 16 shows optimization progress, and Section 7.4 compares a surface-matched FEM hanger.

Seven-stone placement.

We optimize the horizontal initial positions of seven affine bodies with fixed shapes. Their detailed surfaces determine the contacts, while the motion system contains only 84 DoFs. Let bbaseb_{\mathrm{base}} identify the bottom reference stone. At frame tt, dt,bd_{t,b} is the Euclidean distance between the horizontal center positions of stone bb and that reference stone. With allowed distance δ\delta, the placement objective is Lstone=∑t∈ℱ∑b≠bbasemax⁡(dt,b−δ,0)2L_{\mathrm{stone}}=\sum_{t\in\mathcal{F}}\sum_{b\neq b_{\mathrm{base}}}\max(d_{t,b}-\delta,0)^{2}, where ℱ\mathcal{F} is the set of observation frames. The base is excluded from the inner sum, and only distances exceeding δ\delta contribute. Optimization starts from horizontally offset stone placements. The first 50 updates use δ=0.01\delta=0.01 to encourage the simulated centers of mass to align horizontally with that of the base stone. The remaining updates use δ=0.15\delta=0.15 to allow a broader set of contact-supported configurations. Both stages take ℱ={t⋆}\mathcal{F}=\{t^{\star}\}, where t⋆t^{\star} is the first frame where dt,b>δd_{t,b}>\delta for any non-base stone. If dt,b≤δd_{t,b}\leq\delta for every non-base stone at every simulated frame, the loss is zero. The optimizer adjusts the stones’ initial horizontal positions. The loss is computed from the horizontal distances between their simulated centers of mass and that of the base stone. Figure 1 shows updates 10, 50, and 78, with separate 1,000-frame forward simulations testing whether the resulting stacks remain stable. The task demonstrates contact-aware placement through affine initial-state gradients: detailed surface interactions guide the horizontal positions without changing the stones’ shapes.

7.3. Articulated control

Articulated tasks extend the coupled gradients from geometry and placement to actuation. Grasp-angle control tests joint-target tracking under contact, and cup catching optimizes joint commands for the motion of an interacting object. Dual-arm grasping optimizes one vertical offset added to both grippers’ target positions to control their normal contact force on the cloth. These objectives span motion and force while sharing the coupled FEM-affine backward computation.

Grasp-angle control.

An articulated affine robot approaches and grasps a FEM object above a fixed support. The closure objective measures two revolute joints in each finger linkage. The 120-frame horizon includes approach, closure, and return motion. Let 𝒥f\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{f}} be this set of four gripper joints and αt,j\alpha_{t,j} their simulated revolute angles. At the closure observation t=60t=60, the objective is Lgrasp=12​∑j∈𝒥f(α60,j−a∗)2L_{\mathrm{grasp}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{f}}}(\alpha_{60,j}-a^{*})^{2}, with fixed desired angle a∗=0.45a^{*}=0.45 rad. The optimized input is the common target angle. The four angles α60,j\alpha_{60,j} are measured from the simulated response to that target and need not be identical under contact. The optimized joint-target angle is 0.4478430.447843 rad. The objective acts on the four simulated angles, so the gradient accounts for the robot’s response to the command within the coupled scene. Figure 13 compares the grasps. Its dashed guides are visual references and do not enter the loss.

Cup catching.

Joint targets move a plate held firmly by an xArm gripper. The task requires the plate motion to account for the incoming cup’s response through contact. A uniformly decelerating free-plate trajectory, constructed from the cup’s initial velocity, supplies an initial joint-target motion through sequential URDF inverse kinematics (IK). This initializes the commands geometrically. Differentiable simulation then optimizes their effect on the coupled cup-and-plate dynamics, as compared with the stationary and initial-trajectory cases in Figure 14.

The simulation uses 240 frames at h=0.005h=0.005 s with friction coefficient 1.01.0. The optimized command matrix is 𝐔cmd=(𝐮1,…,𝐮100)𝖳∈ℝ100×7\mathbf{U}_{\mathrm{cmd}}=(\mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{100})^{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{100\times 7}, where 𝐮k∈ℝ7\mathbf{u}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{7} contains the relative target angles of the seven arm joints at control sample kk. The command at simulation frame tt is

𝐚tcmd={𝟎,1≤t≤98,𝐮t−98,99≤t≤198,𝐮100,199≤t≤240.\mathbf{a}_{t}^{\mathrm{cmd}}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{0},&1\leq t\leq 98,\\ \mathbf{u}_{t-98},&99\leq t\leq 198,\\ \mathbf{u}_{100},&199\leq t\leq 240.\end{cases}

The final 42 frames hold 𝐮100\mathbf{u}_{100} fixed, and their gradients accumulate into this target.

Five state losses average errors over frames 99–240, starting when the plate commands begin. For body b∈{plate,cup}b\in\{\mathrm{plate},\mathrm{cup}\}, 𝐩tb\mathbf{p}_{t}^{b} and 𝐀tb\mathbf{A}_{t}^{b} denote its simulated center position and affine orientation matrix, and 𝐯tb=(𝐩tb−𝐩t−1b)/h\mathbf{v}_{t}^{b}=(\mathbf{p}_{t}^{b}-\mathbf{p}_{t-1}^{b})/h is its center velocity. Starred plate quantities denote the prescribed reference. Position, velocity, and orientation tracking keep the plate near this path with the intended motion and orientation:

Lp\displaystyle L_{p} =1142​sp2​∑t=99240‖𝐩tplate−𝐩tplate,∗‖2,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{142s_{p}^{2}}\sum_{t=99}^{240}\|\mathbf{p}_{t}^{\mathrm{plate}}-\mathbf{p}_{t}^{\mathrm{plate},*}\|^{2},
Lv\displaystyle L_{v} =1142​sv2​∑t=99240‖𝐯tplate−𝐯tplate,∗‖2,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{142s_{v}^{2}}\sum_{t=99}^{240}\|\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\mathrm{plate}}-\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\mathrm{plate},*}\|^{2},
LA\displaystyle L_{A} =1142​sA2​∑t=99240‖𝐀tplate−𝐀tplate,∗‖F2.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{142s_{A}^{2}}\sum_{t=99}^{240}\|\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{plate}}-\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{plate},*}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}.

The normalization scales are sp=0.02s_{p}=0.02, sv=8s_{v}=\sqrt{8}, and sA=2/20s_{A}={\sqrt{2}}/{20}.

Cup uprightness discourages tipping without constraining yaw, and a relative-velocity loss discourages sliding between the cup and plate. With world up 𝐞up=(−1,0,0)𝖳\mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{up}}=(-1,0,0)^{\mathsf{T}}, the cup up vector is

𝐳tcup=𝐀tcup​(𝐀0cup)−1​𝐞up‖𝐀tcup​(𝐀0cup)−1​𝐞up‖.\mathbf{z}_{t}^{\mathrm{cup}}=\frac{\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{cup}}(\mathbf{A}_{0}^{\mathrm{cup}})^{-1}\mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{up}}}{\|\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{cup}}(\mathbf{A}_{0}^{\mathrm{cup}})^{-1}\mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{up}}\|}.

The two losses are

Lup\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{up}} =1142​∑t=99240‖𝐳tcup−𝐞up‖2,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{142}\sum_{t=99}^{240}\|\mathbf{z}_{t}^{\mathrm{cup}}-\mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{up}}\|^{2},
Lvel\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{vel}} =1142​sv2​∑t=99240‖𝐯tcup−𝐯tplate‖2.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{142s_{v}^{2}}\sum_{t=99}^{240}\|\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\mathrm{cup}}-\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\mathrm{plate}}\|^{2}.

Command smoothness is encouraged by LΔ=199​∑k=2100‖𝐮k−𝐮k−1‖2L_{\Delta}=\frac{1}{99}\sum_{k=2}^{100}\|\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{k-1}\|^{2}, which penalizes changes between consecutive independent targets. The total objective is

Lcup=\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{cup}}={} wp​Lp+wv​Lv+wA​LA\displaystyle w_{p}L_{p}+w_{v}L_{v}+w_{A}L_{A}
+wup​Lup+wvel​Lvel+wΔ​LΔ,\displaystyle+w_{\mathrm{up}}L_{\mathrm{up}}+w_{\mathrm{vel}}L_{\mathrm{vel}}+w_{\Delta}L_{\Delta},

with fixed weights wp=100w_{p}=100, wv=20w_{v}=20, wA=20w_{A}=20, wup=20w_{\mathrm{up}}=20, wvel=50w_{\mathrm{vel}}=50, and wΔ=0.001w_{\Delta}=0.001.

The cup tilt is αt=arccos⁡((𝐳tcup)𝖳​𝐞up)\alpha_{t}=\arccos((\mathbf{z}_{t}^{\mathrm{cup}})^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{up}}). A catch is successful when, in each of the final ten frames, αt≤π/18\alpha_{t}\leq\pi/18 rad, the minimum cup–plate vertex distance is at most 22 mm, and both center speeds ‖𝐯tcup‖\|\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\mathrm{cup}}\| and ‖𝐯tplate‖\|\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\mathrm{plate}}\| are below 0.050.05 m/s. Optimization stops once all of these conditions are met. The optimized plate catches and retains the cup (Figure 14). All 700 joint-target variables are optimized jointly through the arm dynamics and cup–plate contact. Their gradients share one coupled adjoint solve per frame (Sections 4.3 and 5.4). At a fixed simulation horizon, additional control variables therefore require local derivative accumulation rather than additional coupled solves.

Dual-arm towel grasp.

The same vertical offset is added to both grippers’ target positions during descent and the subsequent hold. Optimizing this one value changes how firmly the fingers press the cloth. The horizontal trajectories and finger-closing commands remain fixed. Let F120F_{120} be the total normal contact force between the cloth and the fingers of both arms at frame 120 during the hold.

The target normal force is estimated from the friction needed to accelerate the cloth with the closing fingers, using the cloth mass, prescribed closing acceleration, and cloth–finger friction coefficient. A fixed factor of three provides additional margin, giving F∗=1.4573F^{*}=1.4573 N. The optimized loss is Lforce=12​(F120−F∗)2L_{\mathrm{force}}=\tfrac{1}{2}(F_{120}-F^{*})^{2}, with F120F_{120} measured from the simulated contacts. Starting from a finger-surface height of 1.91.9 mm and contact force 0.02260.0226 N, the optimizer produces a grasp that lifts and folds the towel after seven updates (Figure 15). This task uses a force objective during the press-down hold to set the contact needed for the subsequent cloth motion, linking an affine position command to a deformable-object outcome.

These outcomes connect parameter choice to physical effect: rest geometry establishes support, initial placement forms a stable assembly, and actuation controls contacting objects. All use the same coupled backward equations, with task-specific parameter maps and losses. Figure 16 complements the physical sequences with the corresponding optimization histories.

7.4. Gradient validation and representation studies

Gradient validation.

Table 2 reports finite-difference (FD) checks at the initial optimization parameters for all DiffGIPC examples and the shared DiffIPC benchmarks. For the checked parameter vector 𝐳\mathbf{z}, let 𝐠ana{\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{ana}}} be its analytic loss gradient. The direction 𝐝\mathbf{d} is the normalized gradient, or its sign for a scalar parameter. With perturbation size ϵFD\epsilon_{\mathrm{FD}}, the centered difference is DFD​L=[L⁡(𝐳+ϵFD​𝐝)−L⁡(𝐳−ϵFD​𝐝)]/(2​ϵFD)D_{\mathrm{FD}}L=[L(\mathbf{z}+\epsilon_{\mathrm{FD}}\mathbf{d})-L(\mathbf{z}-\epsilon_{\mathrm{FD}}\mathbf{d})]/(2\epsilon_{\mathrm{FD}}). The reported relative error is |𝐠ana𝖳​𝐝−DFD​L|/max⁡(|𝐠ana𝖳​𝐝|,|DFD​L|)|{\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{ana}}}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{d}-D_{\mathrm{FD}}L|/\max(|{\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{ana}}}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{d}|,|D_{\mathrm{FD}}L|). The shared-case checks use the first 10 frames. The other checks use the stated task-specific windows.

Bunny resolution study.

Table 3 compares three body representations as bunny resolution increases. FEM+FEM uses two deformable bodies, ABD+FEM uses one affine and one FEM body, and ABD+ABD uses two affine bodies. As resolution grows from 933 to 28,435 vertices, the combined forward and backward time for DiffGIPC FEM+FEM increases from 0.98 to 10 s, whereas the ABD+ABD time increases from 0.14 to 0.37 s. The increases are about 10.0×10.0\times and 2.6×2.6\times, respectively.

At the highest resolution, ABD+ABD has a forward-plus-backward speedup of about 27×27\times over DiffGIPC FEM+FEM. The time spent in backward linear solves falls from 2.3 to 0.0044 s (about 520×520\times), while the time for a complete backward evaluation falls from 2.5 to 0.048 s (about 52×52\times). With twelve motion DoFs per body, ABD reduces the adjoint-system size without simplifying the surface mesh used for contact and shape derivatives. For FEM+FEM, the speedup of DiffGIPC over DiffIPC grows from 25.4×25.4\times to 150.0×150.0\times across resolutions. Combining GPU execution with an affine motion representation gives a 4133.3×4133.3\times speedup for DiffGIPC ABD+ABD over DiffIPC FEM+FEM at the highest resolution.

Garment Hanger: ABD versus FEM

This comparison keeps the surface discretization fixed at 4,476 vertices and 8,952 triangles while changing the motion representation. The FEM replacement adds 902 interior vertices and 18,256 tetrahedra, with a harmonic extension of the two Bézier shape fields to the interior. The mean forward-plus-backward cost is 7.1 s for ABD and 1616 s for FEM, giving a speedup of 2.2×2.2\times. The backward costs are 0.27 and 1.01.0 s. The corresponding optimized control-point scales (sx,sy)(s_{x},s_{y}) are (0.8285,0.8000)(0.8285,0.8000) and (0.8301,0.8000)(0.8301,0.8000). At fixed surface discretization, the two models allocate computation differently. FEM resolves non-affine deformation through an interior tetrahedral mesh, whereas ABD retains a compact motion state and differentiates mass directly from the surface. The timings compare forward and backward evaluations of the ABD and FEM models for the same cloth-support design task.

7.5. GPU execution and optimization cost

This section measures the speedup from CUDA Graphs and the time spent on forward simulation and backward differentiation during optimization. Conditional CUDA Graphs reduce coordination during PCG, while parallel assembly and derivative accumulation process the local work surrounding each solve. Table 4 gives a detailed breakdown of the time spent on forward simulation and backward differentiation, together with the evaluation counts and accumulated evaluation time for each optimization. Table 5 compares execution with CUDA Graphs enabled and disabled, reporting PCG and total evaluation times for forward simulation and backward differentiation, together with the resulting speedups.

CUDA Graph execution provides 1.41.4–1.8×1.8\times speedups in forward PCG and 1.31.3–1.8×1.8\times in backward PCG over conventional kernel launches (Table 5). The PCG recurrence and convergence criterion are unchanged. These gains demonstrate the benefit of reducing kernel-launch overhead and CPU–GPU synchronization within the iterative solve (Section 6.1).

PCG is the largest contributor to backward time in most tasks (Table 4), making the adjoint solver a major source of savings in gradient evaluation. The acceleration remains visible in the complete computation: combined forward and backward evaluations achieve 1.21.2–1.5×1.5\times speedups across all reported tasks. These timings include collision detection, Hessian assembly, line search, and derivative accumulation, demonstrating a reduction in the cost of simulation and differentiation beyond the PCG loop itself.

CUDA Graphs also accelerate the additional forward simulations used to evaluate candidate parameters and verify the optimized motion. Grasp-angle optimization, for example, uses 4444 forward evaluations and 2020 backward evaluations (Table 4). The same graph-based forward solver serves both the trajectories used for gradient computation and the additional objective checks and verification runs. Together with the representation study, these results establish complementary benefits: compact coordinates reduce the numerical workload, and graph-based execution reduces the recurring overhead of solving these systems throughout optimization.

8. Conclusion and Discussion

DiffGIPC combines mixed-coordinate trajectory adjoints with GPU execution for contact-rich inverse problems. Full-space FEM and twelve-DoF affine bodies remain coupled through contact, friction, and joints, while affine shape and control derivatives expose these interactions to optimization. Parallel accumulation, CUDA Graph-based PCG, and a PyTorch interface provide the GPU backward and task-level pipeline. Across the shared full-space FEM benchmarks, complete backward evaluation is 12.312.3–34.1×34.1\times faster than DiffIPC, with 10.610.6–60.9×60.9\times combined forward-and-backward speedups. Affine coordinates provide further savings when near-rigid motion is appropriate, although surface resolution still determines contact and assembly work.

Differentiation uses the contact pairs, closest-feature choices, and control operations recorded during forward simulation. A pair of objects that remains outside the barrier’s activation range contributes no direct contact gradient, which can limit the guidance available when the initial trajectory does not establish the desired interaction. Rest-shape derivatives assume fixed connectivity within each differentiated trajectory. Remeshing can occur between optimization steps, but its decisions and vertex transfers are not differentiated. Improving the underlying contact model and the gradients used for optimization offers a direction for future work. Geometric Contact Potential (Huang et al., 2025b) could reduce spurious contact forces and sensitivity to surface discretization. Long-range contact potentials (Ye et al., 2026) could provide gradient information before objects enter the local barrier range, helping optimization establish new contacts. Randomized smoothing with bundled gradients (Suh et al., 2022) could mitigate rapid changes in contact gradients. Adapting these approaches to coupled FEM-affine dynamics and evaluating their effects on simulation accuracy, optimization convergence, and computational cost remain future work.

Appendix A Derivatives for the Coupled FEM–Affine Adjoint

The frame-wise adjoint requires local derivatives for assembling the coupled Hessian and accumulating parameter and earlier-state gradients (Sections 4–6.2). This appendix derives these quantities for friction, elasticity, inertia, and joints. The derivations account for current and previous contact geometry, the dependence of mass and elastic response on rest shape, and the effects of joint geometry and control parameters.

A.1. Friction derivatives

A.1.1. Smoothed friction energy

The friction energy uses current-step sliding and contact quantities computed from previous-frame geometry (Li et al., 2020). For contact cc, the previous positions 𝐱t−1c\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{c} determine the closest-point interpolation weights, contact plane, and normal force. Let 𝐱j−=𝐱t−1,ij\mathbf{x}_{j}^{-}=\mathbf{x}_{t-1,i_{j}} and Δ​𝐱j=𝐱t,ij−𝐱j−\Delta\mathbf{x}_{j}=\mathbf{x}_{t,i_{j}}-\mathbf{x}_{j}^{-} denote the previous position and displacement of contact vertex jj.

The matrix 𝐖∈ℝ3×3​nc\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3n_{c}} converts stacked vertex displacements into the relative displacement of the two closest points:

𝐖=[w1fr𝐈3⋯wncfr𝐈3],𝐖(𝐱tc−𝐱t−1c)=∑j=1ncwjfrΔ𝐱j.\mathbf{W}=[w_{1}^{\mathrm{fr}}\mathbf{I}_{3}\ \cdots\ w_{n_{c}}^{\mathrm{fr}}\mathbf{I}_{3}],\qquad\mathbf{W}\,(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}-\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{c})=\sum_{j=1}^{n_{c}}w_{j}^{\mathrm{fr}}\Delta\mathbf{x}_{j}.

Adding the same displacement to all contact vertices leaves their relative displacement unchanged because the sum of the weights is zero. With 𝒘fr=(w1fr,…,wncfr)\boldsymbol{w}^{\mathrm{fr}}=(w_{1}^{\mathrm{fr}},\ldots,w_{n_{c}}^{\mathrm{fr}}), the weights for the four mesh-contact types of IPC are

𝒘fr={(1,−1),point–point,(1,η−1,−η),point–edge,(1,−β1,−β2,−β3),point–triangle,(1−sA,sA,sB−1,−sB),edge–edge.\boldsymbol{w}^{\mathrm{fr}}=\begin{cases}(1,-1),&\text{point--point},\\ (1,\eta-1,-\eta),&\text{point--edge},\\ (1,-\beta_{1},-\beta_{2},-\beta_{3}),&\text{point--triangle},\\ (1-s_{A},s_{A},s_{B}-1,-s_{B}),&\text{edge--edge}.\end{cases}

The point is numbered first for point–edge and point–triangle contact. For point–edge contact, the other side has endpoints 2,32,3, and its closest point is 𝐱2−+η​𝐞\mathbf{x}_{2}^{-}+\eta\mathbf{e}, where 𝐞=𝐱3−−𝐱2−\mathbf{e}=\mathbf{x}_{3}^{-}-\mathbf{x}_{2}^{-} and η=𝐞𝖳​(𝐱1−−𝐱2−)/(𝐞𝖳​𝐞)\eta=\mathbf{e}^{\mathsf{T}}(\mathbf{x}_{1}^{-}-\mathbf{x}_{2}^{-})/(\mathbf{e}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{e}). For point–triangle contact, β1,β2,β3\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3} are the barycentric coordinates of the closest point on triangle (2,3,4)(2,3,4):

𝐄△\displaystyle\mathbf{E}_{\triangle} =[𝐱3−−𝐱2−𝐱4−−𝐱2−],\displaystyle=[\,\mathbf{x}_{3}^{-}-\mathbf{x}_{2}^{-}\quad\mathbf{x}_{4}^{-}-\mathbf{x}_{2}^{-}\,],
[β2β3]\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}\beta_{2}\\ \beta_{3}\end{bmatrix} =(𝐄△𝖳𝐄△)−1𝐄△𝖳(𝐱1−−𝐱2−),β1=1−β2−β3.\displaystyle=(\mathbf{E}_{\triangle}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{E}_{\triangle})^{-1}\mathbf{E}_{\triangle}^{\mathsf{T}}(\mathbf{x}_{1}^{-}-\mathbf{x}_{2}^{-}),\qquad\beta_{1}=1-\beta_{2}-\beta_{3}.

For edge–edge contact, the two edges have endpoints (1,2)(1,2) and (3,4)(3,4), with closest points 𝐱1−+sA​𝐞A\mathbf{x}_{1}^{-}+s_{A}\mathbf{e}_{A} and 𝐱3−+sB​𝐞B\mathbf{x}_{3}^{-}+s_{B}\mathbf{e}_{B}, where 𝐞A=𝐱2−−𝐱1−\mathbf{e}_{A}=\mathbf{x}_{2}^{-}-\mathbf{x}_{1}^{-} and 𝐞B=𝐱4−−𝐱3−\mathbf{e}_{B}=\mathbf{x}_{4}^{-}-\mathbf{x}_{3}^{-}. The coefficients satisfy

[𝐞A𝖳​𝐞A−𝐞A𝖳​𝐞B−𝐞A𝖳​𝐞B𝐞B𝖳​𝐞B]​[sAsB]=[𝐞A𝖳​(𝐱3−−𝐱1−)−𝐞B𝖳​(𝐱3−−𝐱1−)].\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{e}_{A}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{e}_{A}&-\mathbf{e}_{A}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{e}_{B}\\ -\mathbf{e}_{A}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{e}_{B}&\mathbf{e}_{B}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{e}_{B}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}s_{A}\\ s_{B}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{e}_{A}^{\mathsf{T}}(\mathbf{x}_{3}^{-}-\mathbf{x}_{1}^{-})\\ -\mathbf{e}_{B}^{\mathsf{T}}(\mathbf{x}_{3}^{-}-\mathbf{x}_{1}^{-})\end{bmatrix}.

The edge and triangle formulas apply when the closest points lie in the interiors of the respective features. When a closest point lies at an edge endpoint or on a triangle boundary, the contact uses the corresponding point–point or point–edge formula.

The columns of 𝐔∈ℝ3×2\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 2} are two orthogonal unit directions in the contact plane. In this case, 𝐖=𝐈3\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{I}_{3} and 𝐔=[𝐞x𝐞z]\mathbf{U}=[\,\mathbf{e}_{x}\quad\mathbf{e}_{z}\,], with 𝐞x=(1,0,0)𝖳\mathbf{e}_{x}=(1,0,0)^{\mathsf{T}} and 𝐞z=(0,0,1)𝖳\mathbf{e}_{z}=(0,0,1)^{\mathsf{T}}.

For mesh–mesh contact, 𝐖\mathbf{W} and 𝐔\mathbf{U} depend on 𝐱t−1c\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{c}. Both remain fixed when differentiating with respect to current positions. For the stacked displacement Δ​𝐱tc=𝐱tc−𝐱t−1c\Delta\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}=\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}-\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{c}, the sliding displacement is

(66) 𝝃=𝐔𝖳​𝐖​Δ​𝐱tc,σ=‖𝝃‖2.\boldsymbol{\xi}=\mathbf{U}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{W}\,\Delta\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c},\qquad\sigma=\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|^{2}.

A.1.2. Friction-coefficient and history derivatives

Point-space friction gradient supports coefficient fitting and differentiation through time. Its coefficient derivative measures how frictional resistance changes with μfr\mu_{\mathrm{fr}}. Its history derivative also accounts for changes in closest-point weights, contact-plane orientation, normal force, and relative displacement. Let 𝐠ξ=2​φ′​(σ)​𝝃\mathbf{g}_{\xi}=2\varphi^{\prime}(\sigma)\boldsymbol{\xi} denote the two-dimensional slip derivative in Equation (70). At fixed frame configurations, 𝐖\mathbf{W}, 𝐔\mathbf{U}, and fnf_{n} are independent of μfr\mu_{\mathrm{fr}}. The coefficient derivative and its loss-gradient contribution Δ​μ¯fr(t,c)\Delta\bar{\mu}_{\mathrm{fr}}^{(t,c)} from contact cc at frame tt are

(72) ∂𝐠t,cfr,x∂μfr\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}}{\partial\mu_{\mathrm{fr}}} =fn​𝐖𝖳​𝐔𝐠ξ,\displaystyle=f_{n}\mathbf{W}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{U}\mathbf{g}_{\xi},
Δ​μ¯fr(t,c)\displaystyle\Delta\bar{\mu}_{\mathrm{fr}}^{(t,c)} =−(∂𝐠t,cfr,x∂μfr)𝖳​𝐊t,c​𝝀t.\displaystyle=-\left(\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}}{\partial\mu_{\mathrm{fr}}}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{K}_{t,c}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t}.

The contributions Δ​μ¯fr(t,c)\Delta\bar{\mu}_{\mathrm{fr}}^{(t,c)} are summed over all contacts and frames that share μfr\mu_{\mathrm{fr}}. Together with the direct loss derivative, this sum gives the total coefficient gradient μ¯fr\bar{\mu}_{\mathrm{fr}} in Equation (30).

A change in 𝐱t−1c\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{c} changes both the measured displacement and the geometry defining friction. The corresponding matrix is

(73) 𝐂t,cfr,x=∂𝐠t,cfr,x∂𝐱t−1c∈ℝ3​nc×3​nc.\mathbf{C}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}=\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}}{\partial\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{c}}\in\mathbb{R}^{3n_{c}\times 3n_{c}}.

With the contact vertices indices and contact type fixed, vary 𝐱t−1c\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{c} while holding 𝐱tc\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}, μfr{\mu_{\mathrm{fr}}}, and ϵfr\epsilon_{\mathrm{fr}} fixed. Since d⁡(Δ​𝐱tc)=−d​𝐱t−1c\mathrm{d}(\Delta\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c})=-\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{c}, Equation (66) gives

+μfr​fn​(d​𝐖)𝖳​𝐔𝐠ξ\displaystyle+{\mu_{\mathrm{fr}}}f_{n}(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{W})^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{U}\mathbf{g}_{\xi}
+μfr​fn​𝐖𝖳​(d​𝐔)​𝐠ξ\displaystyle+{\mu_{\mathrm{fr}}}f_{n}\mathbf{W}^{\mathsf{T}}(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{U})\mathbf{g}_{\xi}
+μfr​fn​𝐖𝖳​𝐔𝐇ξ​d​𝝃.\displaystyle+{\mu_{\mathrm{fr}}}f_{n}\mathbf{W}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{U}\mathbf{H}_{\xi}\,\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\xi}.

The weight differential is d𝐖=[(dw1fr)𝐈3⋯(dwncfr)𝐈3]\mathrm{d}\mathbf{W}=[(\mathrm{d}w_{1}^{\mathrm{fr}})\mathbf{I}_{3}\ \cdots\ (\mathrm{d}w_{n_{c}}^{\mathrm{fr}})\mathbf{I}_{3}]. For the remaining contact types, the interpolation weights depend on the previous-frame vertex positions through the closest-point parameters. These parameters locate the closest points on the edges or triangle and form the vector

𝝎cp={[η],point–edge,[β2β3]𝖳,point–triangle,[sAsB]𝖳,edge–edge.\boldsymbol{\omega}_{\mathrm{cp}}=\begin{cases}[\,\eta\,],&\text{point--edge},\\ [\,\beta_{2}\quad\beta_{3}\,]^{\mathsf{T}},&\text{point--triangle},\\ [\,s_{A}\quad s_{B}\,]^{\mathsf{T}},&\text{edge--edge}.\end{cases}

The mapped derivative 𝐊t,c𝖳​𝐂t,cfr,x​𝐊t−1,c\mathbf{K}_{t,c}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{C}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}\mathbf{K}_{t-1,c} places FEM and affine contact points in the same temporal coupling. Second-frame friction therefore contributes to initial-state gradients through the first-frame adjoint. At t=1t=1, the previous positions are initial inputs and their parameter dependence contributes directly to the initial-state gradient.

A.1.3. Rest-shape derivatives under friction

With solved motion DoFs fixed, an affine rest-shape change moves contact points at both the current and previous frames. The direct derivative therefore includes both configurations and the map from point forces to affine DoFs. These derivatives hold 𝐲1,…,𝐲T\mathbf{y}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{y}_{T}, the friction coefficient, and the smoothing threshold fixed. The frame adjoints supply the complementary change in simulated motion.

For a surface vertex ii on affine body bb, let θk=x¯i,a\theta_{k}=\bar{x}_{i,a} be one component of its rest position 𝐱¯i\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i}, where a=1,2,3a=1,2,3 indexes the xx, yy, and zz components, respectively. The vector 𝐞a\mathbf{e}_{a} is the unit vector along the selected coordinate axis. Equation (2) gives ∂𝐱s,i/∂θk=𝐀s,b​𝐞a\partial\mathbf{x}_{s,i}/\partial\theta_{k}=\mathbf{A}_{s,b}\mathbf{e}_{a} at both s=ts=t and s=t−1s=t-1. Thus the same rest-coordinate change moves current and previous contact points through their respective affine transformations. The point map in Equation (3) also changes:

∂𝐉i∂θk=[ 03×3𝐞1​𝐞a𝖳𝐞2​𝐞a𝖳𝐞3​𝐞a𝖳].\frac{\partial\mathbf{J}_{i}}{\partial\theta_{k}}=[\,\mathbf{0}_{3\times 3}\quad\mathbf{e}_{1}\mathbf{e}_{a}^{\mathsf{T}}\quad\mathbf{e}_{2}\mathbf{e}_{a}^{\mathsf{T}}\quad\mathbf{e}_{3}\mathbf{e}_{a}^{\mathsf{T}}\,].

For a contact containing vertex ii, this block occupies the rows of that vertex and the columns of body bb in ∂𝐊t,c/∂θk\partial\mathbf{K}_{t,c}/\partial\theta_{k}. For a shape parameter controlling several rest coordinates, its derivative follows by applying the chain rule through the rest-shape parameterization.

The induced change in the point-space friction gradient is

(74) d​𝐠t,cfr,x=𝐇t,cfr,x​d​𝐱tc+𝐂t,cfr,x​d​𝐱t−1c.\mathrm{d}\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}=\mathbf{H}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}+\mathbf{C}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{c}.

The current-position term uses the Hessian obtained by differentiating Equation (70). The previous-position term uses Equation (73), including the changes in weights, basis, and normal force derived above. Combining these geometry terms with the point-map derivative gives Equation (47). For contact cc at frame tt, the friction contribution Δ​θ¯k(t,c),fr\Delta\bar{\theta}_{k}^{(t,c),\mathrm{fr}} to the loss gradient is

Δ​θ¯k(t,c),fr=\displaystyle\Delta\bar{\theta}_{k}^{(t,c),\mathrm{fr}}={} −(𝐠t,cfr,x)𝖳​∂𝐊t,c∂θk​𝝀t\displaystyle-(\mathbf{g}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x})^{\mathsf{T}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{K}_{t,c}}{\partial\theta_{k}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t}
−(∂𝐱tc∂θk)𝖳​𝐇t,cfr,x​𝐊t,c​𝝀t\displaystyle-\left(\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}}{\partial\theta_{k}}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{H}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x}\mathbf{K}_{t,c}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t}
−(∂𝐱t−1c∂θk)𝖳​(𝐂t,cfr,x)𝖳​𝐊t,c​𝝀t.\displaystyle-\left(\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{c}}{\partial\theta_{k}}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}(\mathbf{C}_{t,c}^{\mathrm{fr},x})^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{K}_{t,c}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t}.

The three terms account for the force map and the contact geometry at both time levels. Their sum over the relevant contacts and frames is added to the other physical contributions and any direct loss derivative to obtain the total rest-shape gradient θ¯k\bar{\theta}_{k}.

For free FEM vertices, the solved positions are the motion DoFs and their point maps are identity matrices. The effect of rest shape on simulated motion is propagated through the frame adjoints. Affine surfaces also contribute the direct geometry and point-map derivatives above. If rest shape determines the initial vertex positions, their direct contribution is included in the first-frame friction derivatives with respect to those initial positions.

A.2. Volumetric FEM and cloth parameter derivatives

Element energies supply both the frame Hessian and the parameter derivatives needed for material identification and deformable rest-shape design. Volumetric elements use stable Neo-Hookean (Smith et al., 2018). Cloth combines the finite-element Baraff–Witkin (Kim, 2020) with StiffGIPC’s cubic extension penalty. Differentiating these energies with respect to material and rest-shape parameters supplies local gradient contributions at fixed current positions. The coupled adjoint accounts for the resulting deformation and its interactions with other objects.

A.2.1. Tetrahedral elasticity

For a tetrahedron with local vertex indices 0,1,2,30,1,2,3, define its rest and current edge matrices as

𝐃erest\displaystyle\mathbf{D}_{e}^{\mathrm{rest}} =[𝐱¯1−𝐱¯0𝐱¯2−𝐱¯0𝐱¯3−𝐱¯0],\displaystyle=[\,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{1}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\quad\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{2}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\quad\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{3}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\,],

A.2.2. Cloth membrane elasticity

For a nondegenerate triangle with local vertices 0,1,20,1,2, define the rest edges 𝐞¯1=𝐱¯1−𝐱¯0\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{1}=\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{1}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{0} and 𝐞¯2=𝐱¯2−𝐱¯0\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{2}=\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{2}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{0}, and the current edge matrix 𝐃ecur=[𝐱1−𝐱0𝐱2−𝐱0]∈ℝ3×2\mathbf{D}_{e}^{\mathrm{cur}}=[\,\mathbf{x}_{1}-\mathbf{x}_{0}\quad\mathbf{x}_{2}-\mathbf{x}_{0}\,]\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 2}. ψemem\displaystyle\psi_{e}^{\mathrm{mem}} =κestr​[s⁡(r1)+s⁡(r2)]+κeshr​ce2,\displaystyle=\kappa_{e}^{\mathrm{str}}\,[s(r_{1})+s(r_{2})]+\kappa_{e}^{\mathrm{shr}}\,c_{e}^{2},

A.2.3. Cloth bending derivatives

The quadratic bending model of Bergou et al. (2006) uses a geometric matrix determined by the adjacent triangle areas and cotangent weights. This matrix supplies the position gradient, Hessian, and bending-stiffness derivative. Its rest-shape derivative includes changes in both the area normalization and the cotangent weights. An interior cloth edge defines a hinge with rest vertices (𝐱¯0,𝐱¯1,𝐱¯2,𝐱¯3)(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{0},\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{1},\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{2},\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{3}), where 0,10,1 are endpoints and 2,32,3 are opposite vertices. The adjacent rest areas are A1=‖𝐞¯0×𝐞¯1‖/2A_{1}=\|\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{0}\times\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{1}\|/2 and A2=‖𝐞¯0×𝐞¯2‖/2A_{2}=\|\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{0}\times\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{2}\|/2. Rest-shape gradients also account for the mass redistribution induced by geometry changes. at fixed solved states. The second term accounts for parameter-dependent positions or velocities in the predictor. Their products share the same coupled adjoint and can be accumulated without forming the global parameter-derivative matrix, as described in Section 6.2.

A.3. Joint geometry and control derivatives

Joint targets and forces influence the coupled scene through the same frame equations as collision and friction. Geometric constraints maintain the connection between the two bodies pp and cc. The control energy sets a target for the joint’s permitted motion or applies a joint force. Differentiating both energies in affine coordinates preserves their cross-body Hessian blocks, allowing the adjoint to connect a joint command to the response of interacting FEM and affine objects. The local expressions use 𝐪=[𝐪p𝖳,𝐪c𝖳]𝖳∈ℝ24\mathbf{q}=[\mathbf{q}_{p}^{\mathsf{T}},\mathbf{q}_{c}^{\mathsf{T}}]^{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{24} and ∇=∇𝐪\nabla=\nabla_{\mathbf{q}}. Joint anchors, reference directions, and stiffnesses are held fixed when differentiating control parameters.

A material-space anchor 𝐱¯b\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{b} has world position 𝐉b​𝐪b\mathbf{J}_{b}\mathbf{q}_{b}, where 𝐉b=𝐉⁡(𝐱¯b)\mathbf{J}_{b}=\mathbf{J}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{b}) is the point map from Equation (3). A material-space direction 𝐚¯\bar{\mathbf{a}} has no translation component. Its map is

Let 𝚫=𝐉c​𝐪c−𝐉p​𝐪p\boldsymbol{\Delta}=\mathbf{J}_{c}\mathbf{q}_{c}-\mathbf{J}_{p}\mathbf{q}_{p}.

A revolute joint matches two distinct points on its hinge line. A.3.3. Revolute orientation

Revolute actuation is expressed directly in the two bodies’ affine coordinates. Bilinear orientation quantities give explicit gradients and constant cross-body Hessian blocks, retaining the coupled angular response in compact motion coordinates. Let 𝐧b=𝐃⁡(𝐧¯b)​𝐪b\mathbf{n}_{b}=\mathbf{D}(\bar{\mathbf{n}}_{b})\mathbf{q}_{b} and 𝐦b=𝐃⁡(𝐦¯b)​𝐪b\mathbf{m}_{b}=\mathbf{D}(\bar{\mathbf{m}}_{b})\mathbf{q}_{b} be the two transformed reference directions on body b∈{p,c}b\in\{p,c\}. A.3.4. Control derivatives and coupled assembly

The coordinate derivatives determine the Hessians of the joint energies in Section 5.4 with respect to the motion DoFs. Differentiating the energy gradients with respect to joint targets and joint forces gives the control derivatives. For a prismatic joint, the scalar multiplying ∇ξ\nabla\xi is k⁡(ξ−a)−fk(\xi-a)-f. Its derivatives with respect to aa and ff are −k-k and −1-1, giving Equation (53). For a revolute target, ∂aSr=−Cr\partial_{a}S_{\mathrm{r}}=-C_{\mathrm{r}} and ∂aCr=Sr\partial_{a}C_{\mathrm{r}}=S_{\mathrm{r}}. Differentiating their state gradients also gives ∂a∇Sr=−∇Cr\partial_{a}\nabla S_{\mathrm{r}}=-\nabla C_{\mathrm{r}} and ∂a∇Cr=∇Sr\partial_{a}\nabla C_{\mathrm{r}}=\nabla S_{\mathrm{r}}. Substitution into the product rule yields Equation (56). The joint-force terms use coordinate gradients −∇ξ-\nabla\xi and −∇α-\nabla\alpha. At fixed aa, ff, and kk, differentiating the state gradients gives the full control-energy Hessians:

(91) 𝐇pri\displaystyle\mathbf{H}^{\mathrm{pri}} =k∇ξ∇ξ𝖳+[k(ξ−a)−f]∇2ξ,\displaystyle=k\nabla\xi\,\nabla\xi^{\mathsf{T}}+[k(\xi-a)-f]\nabla^{2}\xi,
𝐇rev\displaystyle\mathbf{H}^{\mathrm{rev}} =k(∇Sr∇Sr𝖳+Sr∇2Sr)\displaystyle=k(\nabla S_{\mathrm{r}}\nabla S_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathsf{T}}+S_{\mathrm{r}}\nabla^{2}S_{\mathrm{r}})
+kwc(∇Cr∇Cr𝖳−(1−Cr)∇2Cr)\displaystyle+kw_{c}(\nabla C_{\mathrm{r}}\nabla C_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathsf{T}}-(1-C_{\mathrm{r}})\nabla^{2}C_{\mathrm{r}})
−f​∇2​α.\displaystyle-f\nabla^{2}\alpha.

Here wcw_{c} is the fixed cosine weight from Equation (55).

Geometric and control Hessians use the same [𝐪p𝖳,𝐪c𝖳]𝖳[\mathbf{q}_{p}^{\mathsf{T}},\mathbf{q}_{c}^{\mathsf{T}}]^{\mathsf{T}} ordering. Their off-diagonal blocks couple the joint-connected bodies within the frame matrix, alongside the contact blocks coupling them to the rest of the scene. The local control derivative is multiplied by the corresponding free-body entries of the global adjoint in Equation (52). A shared control accumulates contributions from every joint and frame to which it is applied. All selected controls therefore use the same frame adjoints rather than separate coupled solves for individual control variables.

Appendix B Experimental Settings and Parameters

Tables 6 and 7 summarize the simulation settings and differentiated parameter families, respectively, for the experiments in Section 7. The task losses define the observation frames and optimization stopping events. For tasks with separate optimization and verification phases, the differentiated trajectory provides the gradient at the specified observation or event, and the full listed horizon assesses the resulting motion. Forward and backward evaluation counts follow the definitions in Section 7.

For scene diagonal LboxL_{\mathrm{box}}, the collision activation gap is drel​Lboxd_{\mathrm{rel}}L_{\mathrm{box}}, whose square is d^\widehat{d} in the barrier energy. The friction-smoothing velocity d^f\widehat{d}_{f} gives the displacement scale ϵfr=h​d^f\epsilon_{\mathrm{fr}}=h\widehat{d}_{f}. The coefficients κ\kappa and κA\kappa_{\mathrm{A}} control the collision barrier and affine shape energy, respectively. With δ​𝐱\delta\mathbf{x} denoting the Newton search direction in world coordinates, the stopping criterion is

(92) ‖δ​𝐱‖∞<ϵN​h​Lbox.\|\delta\mathbf{x}\|_{\infty}<\epsilon_{N}hL_{\mathrm{box}}.

The shared FEM benchmarks use the same convergence tolerances to align numerical accuracy in the timing comparisons. The forward PCG relative residual tolerance is 10−410^{-4}.

The parameter families in Table 7 connect task-specific design variables to material response, geometry, initial motion, and actuation through the interface in Section 6.3. Different parameterizations and objectives share the same coupled backward computation. Each parameter family is differentiated in its associated motion representation. The FEM rest-shape configuration uses free FEM vertex positions. Affine rest-shape derivatives include the effects of coupled contact and active friction.
